alpine-crown.flavor: When the eagle circles the ridge, the marmots whistle and the whole slope listens. The top of the food web has come home.
alpine-crown.hint: Crown the range with its highest hunter.
alpine-crown.name: Crown of the Range

alpine-haypile.flavor: The pika spends all summer stacking little hay piles for a winter it refuses to sleep through. Tiny animal, enormous work ethic.
alpine-haypile.hint: Welcome the tireless little hay-stacker of the rocks.
alpine-haypile.name: The Haymaker

alpine-reborn.flavor: Goat to ptarmigan to trout in the snowmelt — the whole high country, restored against the wind.
alpine-reborn.name: Graywind Heights Reborn

alpine-restored.flavor: Wildflower turf knitted back over the talus. Up here things grow by the inch and recover by the decade — you sped it up.
alpine-restored.hint: Bring Graywind Heights most of the way back.
alpine-restored.name: Heights Restored

alpine-treeline.flavor: Nothing up here is here by accident. Every one of these has chosen the thin air on purpose.
alpine-treeline.hint: Coax the first hardy few above the trees.
alpine-treeline.name: Above the Treeline

caretaker-of-the-whole.flavor: Every animal in every biome, home. The damaged preserve you inherited is now, simply, wild. The rarest achievement there is.
caretaker-of-the-whole.hint: Welcome home every animal in every biome.
caretaker-of-the-whole.name: Caretaker of the Whole

coastal-keystone.flavor: The textbook keystone species: pull the sea star out and the mussels take everything. Put it back and the whole tidepool shares the rock again.
coastal-keystone.hint: Restore the one animal that holds the whole tidepool together.
coastal-keystone.name: Keystone

coastal-otter.flavor: Otters eat the urchins that eat the kelp — so an otter on the water means a forest under it. Few animals do more with a full belly.
coastal-otter.hint: Welcome the swimmer that keeps the kelp standing.
coastal-otter.name: Otter's Garden

coastal-reborn.flavor: Whale-spout to clam-siphon. The last and wildest stretch of the preserve, complete.
coastal-reborn.name: Pelican Shore Reborn

coastal-restored.flavor: Anchored dunes, full tidepools, kelp in the wrack. The edge of the whole preserve, holding the line against the sea.
coastal-restored.hint: Bring Pelican Shore most of the way back.
coastal-restored.name: Shore Restored

coastal-tide.flavor: Crabs in the wrack line, anemones in the pools, gulls working the surf. The tide was always coming in — now there's a whole shore to meet it.
coastal-tide.hint: Give the tide a shore worth returning to.
coastal-tide.name: The Tide Returns

desert-burrows.flavor: In the desert, real estate is underground. A tortoise digs a burrow and an owl moves into the spare room — nobody wastes a hole here.
desert-burrows.hint: In the desert, the right neighbors share their holes.
desert-burrows.name: Burrow Network

desert-first-life.flavor: Out here life hides from the sun, not in it. The brush and burrows you've built are the first shade anything's had in years.
desert-first-life.hint: Give the heat something to hide in.
desert-first-life.name: Life in the Heat

desert-hunter.flavor: A predator that can wait out the heat means there's finally enough prey to be patient for.
desert-hunter.hint: A hunter that waits out the heat needs prey worth waiting for.
desert-hunter.name: Dryland Hunter

desert-reborn.flavor: The hardest country in the preserve, fully alive — from the elf owl in the cactus to the tarantula under the stone.
desert-reborn.name: Redstone Scrubland Reborn

desert-restored.flavor: Brush and cactus where there was overgrazed flat. You can't flood a desert back — you have to shade it back, and you did.
desert-restored.hint: Bring Redstone Scrubland most of the way back.
desert-restored.name: Scrubland Restored

field-notes.flavor: Page after page of observations. You don't just bring animals back — you sit with them long enough to learn who they are.
field-notes.hint: Observe your wild neighbors, again and again, all over the preserve.
field-notes.name: Field Notes

forager.flavor: A hundred fallen things picked up and put to use. You've stopped scrounging and started stockpiling.
forager.hint: Gather, and keep gathering — build a real stockpile.
forager.name: Forager

forest-canopy.flavor: Shade on the forest floor again. The big trees you raised will outlive everyone reading their rings.
forest-canopy.hint: Raise Old Hollow Forest most of the way back.
forest-canopy.name: Canopy Restored

forest-cavities.flavor: The big woodpecker carves a hole, uses it once, and leaves it for everyone else. One bird's old home is another's new one.
forest-cavities.hint: Some birds carve homes that others move into — gather that crowd.
forest-cavities.name: Hollow Dwellers

forest-night-shift.flavor: After dark a second forest wakes up. The owl hunts what the day birds never see, and the skunk turns over the leaf litter for grubs.
forest-night-shift.hint: Wake the forest that only stirs after dark.
forest-night-shift.name: Night Shift

forest-reborn.flavor: From a logged-over silence to a full, layered wood — floor, understory, canopy, and every wing in between.
forest-reborn.name: Old Hollow Forest Reborn

forest-understory.flavor: Ferns, shrubs, a squirrel arguing with a woodpecker, newts under the deadwood. A forest is built from the ground up, not the canopy down.
forest-understory.hint: Rebuild the forest floor, layer by layer.
forest-understory.name: Understory Returns

full-house.flavor: A hundred kinds of neighbor. The preserve isn't recovering anymore — it's thriving.
full-house.name: Full House

fully-equipped.flavor: Top-tier gear for top-tier work. There's nothing left in the preserve you can't carry, dig, or water.
fully-equipped.hint: Carry your basket, shovel, and watering can to their peak.
fully-equipped.name: Fully Equipped

green-thumb.flavor: Ten living things in soil you readied yourself. Half of restoration is just patience with a watering can.
green-thumb.hint: Put down roots — plant, and plant again.
green-thumb.name: Green Thumb

landscaper.flavor: You don't find the right land — you shape it. Beds, banks, ponds, lakes, and rivers, all on purpose.
landscaper.hint: Shape soil and water across the preserve, tirelessly.
landscaper.name: Landscaper

makers-hands.flavor: Ten things built by hand. Habitat isn't found — it's made, one piece at a time.
makers-hands.hint: Keep crafting; one item won't restore a meadow.
makers-hands.name: Maker's Hands

master-builder.flavor: A hundred and fifty pieces of habitat, placed by hand. The whole preserve has your fingerprints on it.
master-builder.hint: Place habitat until the whole preserve bears your hand.
master-builder.name: Master Builder

master-gardener.flavor: Seventy-five living things put in the ground, sprout by patient sprout. Restoration is mostly just showing up with a watering can.
master-gardener.hint: Plant on a scale that changes the land.
master-gardener.name: Master Gardener

meadow-apex.flavor: A fox only settles where there are voles and rabbits to hunt — so its arrival means the whole chain beneath it is finally fed.
meadow-apex.hint: A meadow is whole when its top hunter trusts it.
meadow-apex.name: Apex of the Grass

meadow-first-bloom.flavor: Grasshopper, then a bee, then a sparrow that eats both, then a fox that eats the sparrow. A food web is just neighbors who need each other.
meadow-first-bloom.hint: Coax the meadow well past its first lonely visitor.
meadow-first-bloom.name: First Bloom

meadow-mender.flavor: The dust is gone. Where you started there was bare ground; now there's a meadow that hums.
meadow-mender.hint: Heal Willow Meadow most of the way back.
meadow-mender.name: Meadow Mender

meadow-pollinators.flavor: Monarch, bumblebee, leafcutter, lady beetle, painted lady — the unpaid workforce that turns flowers into seeds and seeds into more meadow.
meadow-pollinators.hint: Bring back the meadow's little winged workforce.
meadow-pollinators.name: Pollinator Highway

meadow-reborn.flavor: Every animal that belongs here is home. The meadow doesn't need you to hum anymore — but it remembers who started it.
meadow-reborn.name: Willow Meadow Reborn

naturalist.flavor: Twelve books on the shelf — a guide to every area and the annotated edition beside it. You don't just host wildlife now, you understand it.
naturalist.hint: Write up every area's field guide, and its expanded edition.
naturalist.name: Naturalist

open-road.flavor: The first trail gate swings open. One healed meadow, and the whole preserve starts to feel reachable.
open-road.hint: Heal one biome enough to open the next trail.
open-road.name: Open Road

perfectly-equipped.flavor: Basket, shovel and can carried as far as they go. The land answers a little faster now.
perfectly-equipped.hint: Carry your basket, shovel, and watering can all the way to tier 7.
perfectly-equipped.name: Perfectly Equipped

recipe-collector.flavor: Seventy-five different things, each built at least once. You've used nearly every tool on the bench.
recipe-collector.hint: Build a little of almost everything on the bench.
recipe-collector.name: Recipe Collector

steady-hand.flavor: No biome left to languish while you favored another. Every place you've opened is in good health at once.
steady-hand.hint: Keep every area you've opened in good health at the same time.
steady-hand.name: Steady Hand

three-restored.flavor: Three damaged places, brought most of the way home. The preserve is tipping from recovering to recovered.
three-restored.hint: Bring several different biomes most of the way back.
three-restored.name: Halfway Wild

trailblazer.flavor: Every gate open, every trail walked. From your tent to the sea, it's all connected now.
trailblazer.hint: Open every trail in the preserve.
trailblazer.name: Trailblazer

waterworks.flavor: Beds dug, ground watered, the first pools shaped. Wet ground is the difference between bare dirt and a place that holds life.
waterworks.hint: Work the soil and bring it water, again and again.
waterworks.name: Waterworks

welcome-grasshopper.flavor: You saw it through — gathered, built, shaped the land, and welcomed your first neighbor. A single hop in the grass, and you already know how to bring back a whole meadow.
welcome-grasshopper.hint: Every caretaker's journey begins with one small arrival.
welcome-grasshopper.name: First Friend

welcoming-committee.flavor: Fifty species have decided this place is safe again. Word travels fast in the wild.
welcoming-committee.hint: Draw a real crowd back to the preserve.
welcoming-committee.name: Welcoming Committee

well-stocked.flavor: A thousand fallen things gathered. You stopped scrounging long ago — this is provisioning.
well-stocked.hint: Gather far past what any one project needs.
well-stocked.name: Well Stocked

wetland-engineer.flavor: The beaver doesn't move into habitat — it builds it. One dam, and otters, herons, and frogs all get a home they couldn't have made themselves.
wetland-engineer.hint: Welcome the one who builds habitat for everyone else.
wetland-engineer.name: The Engineer

wetland-first-water.flavor: Shape the water and the water brings its own crowd — frogs, striders, dragonflies skating the surface, a heron stalking the shallows.
wetland-first-water.hint: Shape water, and life will find it.
wetland-first-water.name: Water Returns

wetland-lakemaker.flavor: Enough open water to hold a sky. Turtles bask, mergansers dive, and the whole marsh has a center again.
wetland-lakemaker.hint: Open enough connected water to hold a sky.
wetland-lakemaker.name: Lakemaker

wetland-reborn.flavor: Crane to minnow, the whole drained marsh is wet and loud and alive.
wetland-reborn.name: Rushwater Wetland Reborn

wetland-restored.flavor: Reeds where there was cracked mud, channels that actually flow. A wetland filters everything downstream of it — quiet, unpaid work.
wetland-restored.hint: Heal Rushwater Wetland most of the way back.
wetland-restored.name: Marsh Restored

alpine-butterfly.diet: stonecrop as a caterpillar, then nectar from stonecrop and daisies as an adult
alpine-butterfly.fact: Its wings are almost see-through, like waxed paper held up to the light, and the red spots are a warning. Birds that try one usually spit it straight back out.
alpine-butterfly.hint: Nectar keeps the adults hanging around. Stonecrop is what keeps them for good. Plant flowers without the caterpillar's one food plant and all you get is visitors.
alpine-butterfly.name: Alpine Butterfly
alpine-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Rocky open alpine and subalpine slopes where stonecrop grows between the stones
alpine-butterfly.role: A butterfly that flies in air most insects cannot manage. Its caterpillars eat stonecrop and absolutely nothing else, so the butterfly only lives where the stonecrop does, while the adults drift between meadow flowers for nectar. Pipits and bluebirds still catch a few.
alpine-butterfly.shelter: No nest — the caterpillar develops fully inside the egg and overwinters there, hatching at snowmelt

alpine-moth.diet: flower nectar as an adult, drunk after dark; leaves and roots down in the lowlands as a caterpillar
alpine-moth.fact: Every summer millions of these moths fly up out of the lowlands and hide in the rock on the highest peaks. They are so fatty that a bear will spend all day flipping stones to eat them, and can put away forty thousand moths in a single day.
alpine-moth.hint: Flowers to drink from at night and loose slabs to hide under by day. It only shows up in high summer — the rest of the year it is a caterpillar a long way downhill.
alpine-moth.name: Alpine Moth
alpine-moth.preferredHabitat: High rockslides beside flower turf — but only in summer; it spends the rest of the year far below
alpine-moth.role: The mountain's fuel delivery. The moths fatten on lowland flowers, then migrate hundreds of kilometres uphill to sit out the summer in the cold rock, and every one arrives as a little parcel of fat richer than anything else growing up here. Bears, birds and just about everything that hunts a rockslide feeds on them. At night they come out to drink nectar and pollinate high-country flowers; by dawn they are back under the slabs. Break up the loose rock and the whole larder goes with it.
alpine-moth.shelter: Packed by the thousand into cracks under scree slabs, out of the sun and the wind

american-badger.diet: ground squirrels, gophers, voles and mice dug straight out of their tunnels; also insects and bumble bee nests
american-badger.fact: A badger can dig itself completely out of sight in under a minute — and it sometimes hunts alongside a mountain lion, the badger going in from below while the mountain lion grabs whatever bolts out of the top.
american-badger.hint: Deep stone-free soil it can tear through, wide grass on top, and a ground squirrel colony to hunt. Rock piles are the opposite of what it wants.
american-badger.name: American Badger
american-badger.preferredHabitat: Open grassland with deep, stone-free, diggable soil and a rodent colony to work
american-badger.role: A carnivore that hunts by excavation, going down a squirrel or gopher tunnel after its owner. That only works in deep stone-free soil, and only where there is a rodent colony worth the digging. The big holes it leaves behind get reused by foxes, coyotes and burrowing insects for years afterwards. Adults are safe from almost everything; cubs are not.
american-badger.shelter: Digs its own large burrows; one of the fastest excavators alive

american-goldfinch.diet: almost entirely seeds — thistle, sunflower, aster and grass seed
american-goldfinch.fact: Goldfinches are such strict vegetarians that a cowbird chick sneaked into a goldfinch nest starves — it cannot survive on an all-seed diet.
american-goldfinch.hint: Let the sunflowers and native thistles stand and go to seed. The down is what the late nest is lined with, so don't cut them back in autumn.
american-goldfinch.name: American Goldfinch
american-goldfinch.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open ground with native thistle, sunflower and asters left standing
american-goldfinch.role: A seed specialist that waits until midsummer to nest, when thistle down is finally ready to line the cup. It feeds its chicks on seed rather than insects, which almost no other songbird does, and it scatters thistle and sunflower seed across the meadow as it feeds. Being small and everywhere makes it a favourite of bird-catching hawks.
american-goldfinch.shelter: A tight cup nest lashed a few feet up in a shrub, bound with spider silk and lined with thistle down

anchovy.diet: plankton — copepods, diatoms and larvae — strained from the water or picked one at a time
anchovy.fact: An anchovy eats two ways: it snaps at big prey one bite at a time, or just opens its mouth and swims, straining the sea like a living net.
anchovy.hint: Cold water rising from the deep grows the plankton they eat, and quiet shallows give the schools somewhere to spawn.
anchovy.name: Anchovy
anchovy.preferredHabitat: Cool, plankton-rich nearshore water over the shelf
anchovy.role: Anchovies travel in silver schools so thick they turn the water dark from below. Almost everything that hunts here takes them at some point — pelicans, seals, dolphins, gulls — so when the anchovies fail, the whole coast goes hungry at once.
anchovy.shelter: The school itself; open nearshore water, with kelp and surfgrass edges as nursery cover

anemone.diet: crabs, detached mussels and small fish stung by its tentacles
anemone.fact: That glowing green comes from algae living inside the anemone's own body, making sugar out of sunlight and handing it over like rent. An anemone stuck in the shade goes pale and goes hungry.
anemone.hint: A sunlit pool with surge running through it, sitting below a mussel bed. Dinner falls in from upstairs.
anemone.name: Anemone
anemone.preferredHabitat: Clear, sunlit, surge-fed pools in the low zone
anemone.role: A sit-still hunter that waits below the mussel beds and catches whatever the surf knocks loose from above, while farming its own private algae for extra meals. Half its food arrives by accident, falling out of the rocks overhead.
anemone.shelter: The walls and floors of surge-flushed pools, characteristically just below the mussel beds

antelope-squirrel.diet: cactus fruit, seeds and green shoots, with the odd insect
antelope-squirrel.fact: It runs with its tail flipped flat over its back like a tiny parasol, then throws itself belly-down on cool shaded ground to dump the heat it picked up on the way.
antelope-squirrel.hint: Dry seeds alone will not keep it alive — it needs juicy fruit, and that means welcoming the bees first.
antelope-squirrel.name: Antelope Squirrel
antelope-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Rocky ground with cactus in fruit
antelope-squirrel.role: The one animal still out and about at midday, when everything else has gone underground to wait. It cannot make its own water, so it lives on juicy cactus fruit — which only exists if the cactus bees got to the flowers first. Coyotes, kit foxes, hawks, roadrunners and rattlesnakes all hunt it.
antelope-squirrel.shelter: Burrows and cracks under rocks and cactus

bald-eagle.diet: mostly fish, plus ducks, muskrats and carrion — and anything it can bully out of another hunter's grip
bald-eagle.fact: A bald eagle would honestly rather rob than fish. It shadows otters and herons and harasses them until they drop their catch, then takes it — and the nest it rebuilds every year can end up heavier than a small car.
bald-eagle.hint: One huge old tree with a clear view over deep water, enough fish to live on — and successful otters and herons below to steal from.
bald-eagle.name: Bald Eagle
bald-eagle.preferredHabitat: Wide open water full of fish, with one very tall tree to watch it all from
bald-eagle.role: The top predator of the marsh and its biggest bully. It takes fish, ducks and muskrats for itself, kills herons at their nesting colonies, and spends much of the day stealing meals from otters and herons — which means it can only settle somewhere those hunters are already doing well.
bald-eagle.shelter: A huge stick nest in the crown of the tallest living tree beside open water, added to every year

banana-slug.diet: fallen leaves, mushrooms, animal droppings and other decaying matter; occasionally live seedlings
banana-slug.fact: Banana slug slime is a numbing agent — one lick and most animals spit the slug straight back out, tongue tingling.
banana-slug.hint: Deep damp leaves, mossy shade and mushrooms to graze. Skip the pond — this one drinks through its skin, straight out of the litter.
banana-slug.name: Banana Slug
banana-slug.preferredHabitat: Cool, shaded forest floor that stays damp — deep leaf litter, mossy logs and seeps
banana-slug.role: The banana slug is the forest floor's shredder. Fungi and bacteria do the fine chemistry; the slug does the chewing, grinding fallen leaves into wet crumbs that rot far faster and turning a whole autumn of leaves into soft duff. It grazes mushrooms too, and spores ride safely through its gut, so every silver trail plants fungi somewhere new. Gartersnakes and raccoons are two of the very few animals willing to put up with the slime.
banana-slug.shelter: Under logs and loose bark; seals itself into a mucus cocoon and waits out dry spells

barn-owl.diet: almost entirely small mammals under about 100 grams — voles, mice and shrews
barn-owl.fact: A barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness by sound alone. One ear sits higher than the other, so it hears in three dimensions — and the fringed edges of its wings mean the mouse never hears it coming.
barn-owl.hint: A dark loft or a deep box up off the ground, wide grass to quarter over, and a meadow already full of voles. It takes its water from its prey.
barn-owl.name: Barn Owl
barn-owl.preferredHabitat: Wide open grassland to hunt over, with a dark cavity above ground to sleep and nest in
barn-owl.role: The meadow works a night shift, and the barn owl runs it. While the hawk and the mountain lion hunt by daylight, this one quarters the same grass in the dark on silent wings, living almost entirely on voles — a single family can take well over a thousand of them in a year. Nothing here hunts the barn owl back.
barn-owl.shelter: Nests and roosts in a dark high cavity: a barn loft, a hollow tree, or a large nest box. Builds nothing itself

bat-star.diet: algae, detritus, and dead plants and animals
bat-star.fact: A bat star eats by pushing its stomach out through its mouth and spreading it over its meal, digesting food outside its own body. It also refuses to stick to five arms — four to nine is perfectly normal.
bat-star.hint: Broken rock and rubble with surfgrass streaming over it. This is a rocky-bottom animal, not an eelgrass one.
bat-star.name: Bat Star
bat-star.preferredHabitat: Shallow rocky and rubble bottom with surfgrass or kelp
bat-star.role: The cleanup crew of the shallows. It slides over the seafloor digesting algae, scraps and dead animals exactly where they lie, doing the same job a mushroom or an earthworm does on land — just wetter, and with more arms.
bat-star.shelter: Rocky rubble bottoms, surfgrass beds and kelp holdfasts

beach-hopper.diet: decaying kelp and other stranded seaweed in the wrack line
beach-hopper.fact: Beach hoppers spend all day sealed inside a burrow in dry sand, then pour out after dark to shred the seaweed the tide left behind. Step near one and it fires itself into the air like a flicked pebble.
beach-hopper.hint: Leave the seaweed where the tide drops it. That is the whole meal.
beach-hopper.name: Beach Hopper
beach-hopper.preferredHabitat: Gently sloping sandy beach with an undisturbed wrack line
beach-hopper.role: The engine room of the beach. Hoppers chew stranded kelp down into crumbs and nutrients, and in doing so they turn dead seaweed into bird food — which is the entire reason plovers, sanderlings and gulls patrol the tide line. Rake the wrack away and this link vanishes overnight.
beach-hopper.shelter: Burrows dug in damp sand high on the beach, and the damp underside of drift kelp and driftwood

beaver.diet: bark and cambium of willow and aspen, plus cattail rhizomes and submerged plants
beaver.fact: A beaver's front teeth never stop growing and are orange because they are reinforced with iron — living chisels that gnawing keeps sharp. Its lips shut behind those teeth, so it can carry and cut branches underwater without swallowing the pond.
beaver.hint: Willows to fell and eat, a soft bank to den in, and enough water to float a log. Once it settles, seven new habitats become buildable.
beaver.name: Beaver
beaver.preferredHabitat: Slow channels with mud banks and woody plants to fell
beaver.role: The marsh's engineer, and the turning point of the whole restoration. Fell a few willows, dam a channel, and suddenly there is deep permanent water with drowned trees standing in it — the pond the otter, the merganser, the kingfisher, the heron and the eagle all move in on afterwards.

bighorn-sheep.diet: chiefly grasses and sedges, with forbs and woody browse in winter
bighorn-sheep.fact: Rams charge each other and crash horns hard enough to be heard a mile off. Their skulls are double-layered to take the hit, and a lamb is climbing rock within a day of being born.
bighorn-sheep.hint: Good grazing is only half of it. It will not use a slope it cannot escape from, so put the turf right up against broken cliff — and a mineral lick nearby, because it will travel a long way for salt.
bighorn-sheep.name: Bighorn Sheep
bighorn-sheep.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf directly beside steep, broken escape cliffs
bighorn-sheep.role: A cliff-edge grazer that crops turf on open slopes and never feeds further from broken rock than it can sprint. Mountain lions take adults and lambs, and eagles carry newborn lambs off the ledges.
bighorn-sheep.shelter: Beds on rocky ledges and rugged escape terrain near cliffs

black-bear.diet: berries, acorns and nuts above all; also grasses and forbs, insects and grubs, carrion, and fawns in spring
black-bear.fact: Black bear cubs are born in the middle of hibernation, blind and smaller than a soup can, and their mother barely wakes up for it.
black-bear.hint: A full larder and a winter bed: heavy berry crops, acorn-bearing oaks, water, and a den under the tipped-up roots of a fallen tree.
black-bear.name: Black Bear
black-bear.preferredHabitat: Dense forest with a thick understory and reliable berry and acorn crops
black-bear.role: A black bear ties the whole forest together in one animal: berries, acorns, grubs torn out of rotting logs, an elk calf in spring. It carries berry seeds for miles before dropping them, and every log it rips apart rots faster afterwards. A bear's year is really an acorn year — when the mast crop fails bears wander enormous distances, and a forest with no oaks cannot keep them. Nothing here hunts a grown bear.
black-bear.shelter: Winter dens under upturned root masses, in hollow trees and rock cavities, or dug into a bank

black-swift.diet: flying ants, aphids, beetles and mayflies caught on the wing, often hundreds of metres up
black-swift.fact: A black swift can stay in the air for six months without landing once — it eats, drinks and sleeps flying, and the chick is left alone all day while its parents hunt insects 50 km away.
black-swift.hint: Find the wettest, darkest crack in the cliff and keep the water running down it. This one will not nest anywhere it can walk to.
black-swift.name: Black Swift
black-swift.preferredHabitat: Cliffs with cold running water and wide open sky above the treeline
black-swift.role: Swifts hoover up the swarming insects that get lifted onto the mountain by rising air, and they carry that food back as a compressed pellet — one delivery a day is enough for a chick because the load is so concentrated. The nest has to be permanently wet and unreachable, so the birds only appear where there is a cliff seam with water running over it. They are among the very last summer visitors to arrive and the first to leave for the Amazon.
black-swift.shelter: A cup of moss glued to a wet rock seam behind or beside falling water, reached only from the air

black-turnstone.diet: barnacles, limpets, small mussels, hermit crabs and other rocky-shore invertebrates
black-turnstone.fact: A turnstone does exactly what its name promises — flips over stones, shells and clumps of seaweed to snatch whatever is hiding underneath — and hammers barnacles open with a stubby bill shaped like a chisel.
black-turnstone.hint: Barnacle-crusted rock to hammer at when the tide is out, and a high dry rock to stand on when it is not.
black-turnstone.name: Black Turnstone
black-turnstone.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal shores with barnacle and limpet crusts
black-turnstone.role: A rocky-shore forager that pries barnacles and limpets loose and turns over wrack for hidden prey. It also needs somewhere safe to sit out high tide, when every feeding rock it owns is underwater. Take away the roosts and the shore loses its turnstones even with the food untouched.
black-turnstone.shelter: Rocky shoreline; tight flocks on raised rock at high tide

blue-jay.diet: acorns and beechnuts, caterpillars, beetles and other insects, and eggs or nestlings when it finds them
blue-jay.fact: Blue jay feathers are not actually blue — the pigment in them is brown, and the blue is a trick of light bouncing off tiny air pockets. Crush one and the colour disappears.
blue-jay.hint: Oaks and a patch of soft open ground to bury the acorns in. Some of the ones it forgets will be your next oak trees.
blue-jay.name: Blue Jay
blue-jay.preferredHabitat: Oak-rich woodland and its edges, with open ground nearby for caching
blue-jay.role: A single blue jay can carry five acorns at a time and bury a few thousand in an autumn, and it chooses sound ones and pushes them into open ground — which makes jays the fastest tree planters in the forest and the reason oaks spread uphill after a fire. Jays also mimic hawk calls, sometimes to clear a feeding spot and sometimes to warn everything nearby that a real hawk has arrived, so the whole wood listens to them.
blue-jay.shelter: A cup of twigs and rootlets wedged in a fork high in a leafy tree, screened by foliage

bluebird.diet: ground insects — caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers — plus berries in winter
bluebird.fact: A bluebird can spot a caterpillar on the ground from the top of a fencepost twenty metres away, drop on it, and be back on the post before you've noticed it left.
bluebird.hint: It can't make its own hole. Put a box up facing open grass, keep the grass short enough to hunt over, and add berries for the winter.
bluebird.name: Bluebird
bluebird.preferredHabitat: Grassy openings with scattered trees and low perches to drop from
bluebird.role: Bluebirds hunt by perching, staring at short grass, and dropping. They cannot cut their own nest hole, so they take over holes something else made — and in a meadow with no woodpecker, that means a nest box. Volunteers putting up box trails are a large part of why this bird came back at all.
bluebird.shelter: Grass-lined nest inside a tree cavity, an old woodpecker hole or a nest box

bobcat.diet: obligate carnivore: rabbits, squirrels and rodents, plus some birds, reptiles and deer fawns
bobcat.fact: A bobcat can bring down prey eight times its own weight, then bury the leftovers under leaves or snow and come back the next night.
bobcat.hint: Dense understory to stalk through, a sheltered rock den for kittens, and plenty of prey already back.
bobcat.name: Bobcat
bobcat.preferredHabitat: Forest with a dense understory, brushy edges and broken rocky ground
bobcat.role: With no wolves or cougars in these woods, the bobcat is the top hunter on the ground and nothing hunts a grown one. It takes everything from chipmunks up to raccoons, foxes and even fishers, and it kills by ambush — creeping close through cover, then one short rush. Strip the understory and the bobcat leaves, however much prey is still standing around: it has nothing left to hide behind.
bobcat.shelter: Dens under rock ledges, in hollow logs and in dense thickets; a female moves her kittens if disturbed

boreal-toad.diet: beetles, ants, flies, springtails and other invertebrates; tadpoles graze algae
boreal-toad.fact: It spends September to May underground, then comes out and breeds in pools that were solid ice a few weeks earlier.
boreal-toad.hint: Shallow warm pools to breed in and a burrow to spend the other eight months of the year in. Keep the pools fishless, because stocked trout are the single biggest reason high-country amphibians disappear.
boreal-toad.name: Boreal Toad
boreal-toad.preferredHabitat: Subalpine and alpine wet meadows with shallow, sun-warmed, fish-free breeding pools
boreal-toad.role: The only toad living this high. Adults eat insects by the thousand and the tadpoles graze algae in shallow, sun-warmed pools, and almost nothing eats them because their skin tastes foul. What actually threatens this toad is a skin fungus and trout stocked into lakes that never had fish.
boreal-toad.shelter: Rodent burrows, rock chambers and damp cover above the breeding pools

bottlenose-dolphin.diet: schooling fish, especially anchovy, plus squid and bottom fish
bottlenose-dolphin.fact: Every dolphin invents its own signature whistle, and the others copy that whistle back when they want to call it over. Along an open beach these dolphins hunt right inside the breakers, surfing the waves they are herding fish against.
bottlenose-dolphin.hint: Deep water to travel through, cold currents and kelp edges to hold the fish, and a real breaking surf line, because that is where this one does its hunting.
bottlenose-dolphin.name: Bottlenose Dolphin
bottlenose-dolphin.preferredHabitat: Nearshore water along an open beach with a strong surf line and fish schools offshore
bottlenose-dolphin.role: Fast, social hunters that work the surf line in small groups, pushing anchovy schools up against the breaking waves until the fish have nowhere left to go. They are quick and clever enough to catch almost anything that schools here — and still not the biggest thing in the water.
bottlenose-dolphin.shelter: None built — travels and sleeps at sea in a small group, half its brain awake at a time

brant-goose.diet: eelgrass, plus sea lettuce and other green algae
brant-goose.fact: Brant fly thousands of miles to eat basically one thing: eelgrass. Lose the eelgrass in a bay and the geese are gone within a season or two, no matter how nice the rest of it looks.
brant-goose.hint: Eelgrass to graze, and a quiet sandbar to stand on while the tide is too high to feed.
brant-goose.name: Brant Goose
brant-goose.preferredHabitat: Shallow coastal bays with eelgrass beds
brant-goose.role: A small sea goose that grazes eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays and almost nothing else. Because it is so fussy, a bay full of brant is a bay with healthy seagrass — they are a living gauge of the meadow below them.
brant-goose.shelter: Open shoreline, sandbars and shallow bays

brown-bat.diet: night-flying insects, especially beetles, plus moths, flying ants and midges
brown-bat.fact: A big brown bat finds a moth in total darkness by shouting and listening to the echo — and it can pick out something no thicker than a pencil lead this way.
brown-bat.hint: A warm crevice to raise pups in, insects in the air above the grass, and calm open water it can skim a drink from without landing.
brown-bat.name: Brown Bat
brown-bat.preferredHabitat: Open meadow and hedgerow airspace to hunt over, with still water to drink from and a warm roost nearby
brown-bat.role: The night shift over the meadow. Big brown bats work the air above the grass and along the hedgerows after sunset, catching beetles, moths and flying ants; one bat can put away thousands of insects in a single night. They drink on the wing, dipping their jaws into still water without stopping, and mothers gather in warm roosts to raise pups together. Great horned owls catch them at dusk.
brown-bat.shelter: Roosts by day in warm dark spaces — barn lofts, attics, and under loose bark; hibernates in cold cracks

brown-pelican.diet: small schooling fish, especially northern anchovy
brown-pelican.fact: A brown pelican dives from sixty feet up and hits the water hard enough to stun fish — and it twists its body left just before impact so the blow does not break its neck.
brown-pelican.hint: An island the tide and the footpaths cannot reach, sandbars to loaf on, and it schools in the water offshore.
brown-pelican.name: Brown Pelican
brown-pelican.preferredHabitat: Anchovy-rich nearshore water within reach of an island colony
brown-pelican.role: A plunge-diving anchovy hunter whose comeback after pesticide poisoning is one of the great conservation rescues. It nests only on islands offshore, never on the mainland beach, and its colonies fail outright in years when the anchovy schools do not show — so a nesting brown pelican is a statement about the fish, not the sand.
brown-pelican.shelter: Nests only on undisturbed offshore islands; loafs on sandbars and rocks

bumblebee.diet: nectar for fuel and pollen for protein, from a wide range of flowers
bumblebee.fact: Some flowers refuse to let go of their pollen unless they are shaken. A bumblebee grabs on and buzzes its flight muscles until the pollen falls out — tomatoes and blueberries depend on it.
bumblebee.hint: Flowers are only half of it. A queen also needs an abandoned vole hole under a thick grass tussock to start her colony in.
bumblebee.name: Bumblebee
bumblebee.preferredHabitat: Flower-rich meadows with something in bloom from spring to frost
bumblebee.role: Big, furry and warm enough to fly on cold grey mornings when other bees are still grounded, the bumblebee is the meadow's heavy-duty pollinator. A whole colony starts with one queen in spring hunting for an old vole hole to move into, so nest holes matter every bit as much as flowers. Orb weavers and crab spiders take her at the flowers, and badgers dig entire nests out of the ground.
bumblebee.shelter: Nests in abandoned rodent burrows, grass tussocks and ground cavities

burrowing-owl.diet: big insects — termites, grasshoppers and crickets — plus small rodents and scorpions
burrowing-owl.fact: Corner a burrowing owl down its hole and it hisses like a rattlesnake — biologists think it is doing an impression, and whatever is digging usually decides not to.
burrowing-owl.hint: It cannot dig. Bring the tortoise back first and its old den becomes the front door — with low, open ground out front to hunt over.
burrowing-owl.name: Burrowing Owl
burrowing-owl.preferredHabitat: Open ground with low, sparse plants and ready-made burrows
burrowing-owl.role: A long-legged little owl that hunts insects in broad daylight and rodents after dark, standing on its doorstep bobbing at anything that comes near. It is the clearest case here of an animal that cannot make its own home: every pair depends on a burrow something else dug, so where the diggers go, the owls go too.
burrowing-owl.shelter: Underground burrows dug by somebody else; it cannot dig its own

cactus-bee.diet: pollen and nectar from prickly pear and cholla flowers
cactus-bee.fact: Every female digs her own nest and stocks it herself — but thousands of these single mothers dig side by side in the same patch of bare ground, so the whole ground hums.
cactus-bee.hint: Cactus flowers to work and a patch of loose, unpacked ground to dig in. Trampled hardpan is useless to her.
cactus-bee.name: Cactus Bee
cactus-bee.preferredHabitat: Blooming prickly pear and cholla beside open, undisturbed soil
cactus-bee.role: The bee that makes cactus fruit happen. No bee visits means no fruit set, and no fruit means no midsummer water for the squirrels, birds and rodents that live on it. She needs soft, undisturbed bare soil to dig in, which is exactly what hooves and tyres destroy first.
cactus-bee.shelter: A vertical nest shaft dug in bare, loose ground, often with a little mud chimney over the door

cactus-woodpecker.diet: insects, cactus fruit and mistletoe berries
cactus-woodpecker.fact: It chisels a hole into a living cactus and then waits months, doing nothing, while the plant seals the raw walls with hard scar tissue — only then will it move in.
cactus-woodpecker.hint: Tall cactus to carve and split fruit to eat. A pad cactus is far too small — only a great column can hold a nest hole.
cactus-woodpecker.name: Cactus Woodpecker
cactus-woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands with mesquite and washes nearby
cactus-woodpecker.role: The only animal here that can build a home from scratch, and half the biome lives in its leftovers: elf owls, kestrels, flycatchers and wild bees all move into old woodpecker holes. It also eats cactus fruit by the beakful and drops the seeds wherever it goes, so the cactus needs the bird just as much as the bird needs the cactus.
cactus-woodpecker.shelter: Cavities it chisels out of living saguaros

cactus-wren.diet: insects and spiders, with some cactus fruit and seeds
cactus-wren.fact: A cactus wren builds several football-shaped nests and keeps the spare ones as bedrooms all year, so it goes to sleep surrounded on every side by cactus spines.
cactus-wren.hint: Cholla is the nest. Nothing else out here is spiny enough, and it never once needs a drink.
cactus-wren.name: Cactus Wren
cactus-wren.preferredHabitat: Desert with dense cholla and scattered trees
cactus-wren.role: The biggest wren you will ever meet, flipping over leaves and bark for insects and spiders and taking every drop of its water from that food. Its nest sits deep inside a cholla where the spines keep snakes and raiding birds out — take away the cholla and the wren has nowhere at all to raise chicks.
cactus-wren.shelter: Football-shaped grass nests built deep inside a cholla

chipmunk.diet: seeds, acorns, hickory nuts, berries and underground fungi, plus some insects and bird eggs
chipmunk.fact: A chipmunk can cram so many acorns into its cheek pouches that its head looks twice as wide, then unload them into an underground pantry holding more than a litre of seeds. It wakes up all winter to snack — chipmunks never truly hibernate.
chipmunk.hint: A brush pile to bolt into is enough to start with.
chipmunk.name: Chipmunk
chipmunk.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous forest with logs, stumps and diggable soil
chipmunk.role: The chipmunk is a hoarder and a digger. Every seed it carries off and never eats is a seed planted somewhere new, and spores from the fungi it digs up travel with it. Its tunnels loosen and air the soil. Small, common and awake in daylight, it is the prey base almost every predator here is waiting on — which is why so many of them cannot come back until it does.
chipmunk.shelter: Underground burrows up to 10 m long with a nest chamber and a seed-storage larder

chorus-frog.diet: small insects and other tiny invertebrates
chorus-frog.fact: A chorus frog freezes solid every winter. Ice fills the spaces around its organs, its heart stops for weeks — and in spring it thaws out and starts singing as though nothing happened. The call sounds exactly like running your thumb along a comb.
chorus-frog.hint: Shallow water to sing and breed in, and a deep, damp pile of leaves on dry land to spend the winter frozen inside.
chorus-frog.name: Chorus Frog
chorus-frog.preferredHabitat: Shallow pools ringed with reeds and wet meadow
chorus-frog.role: Small enough to sit on a coin and loud enough to hear right across the marsh. It mops up tiny insects all summer and then feeds herons, mink, otters and cranes — the most-eaten voice in the wetland.
chorus-frog.shelter: Damp litter and loose bark under fallen wood in winter; wet vegetation in summer

cottontail-rabbit.diet: grasses and clover in summer; twigs, bark and buds in winter
cottontail-rabbit.fact: A cottontail doesn't dig a burrow. It presses a shallow bowl into the grass called a form and sits so still in it that you can walk straight past.
cottontail-rabbit.hint: A brushy form to bolt into, native grass to graze, and berries close by. It gets most of its water straight out of green plants.
cottontail-rabbit.name: Cottontail Rabbit
cottontail-rabbit.preferredHabitat: Meadows and field edges with brushy cover close enough to run to
cottontail-rabbit.role: Cottontails eat grass and clover all summer and switch to twigs and bark in winter, and they breed fast enough to keep up with everything that hunts them — fox, coyote, badger, hawk and owl all count on them. Their droppings feed the soil life underfoot, which is a polite way of saying rabbits fertilise the meadow they eat.
cottontail-rabbit.shelter: Rests in shallow grass 'forms'; bolts into brush piles and old burrows

coyote.diet: voles, rabbits and ground squirrels; deer fawns; also fruit, insects and carrion
coyote.fact: Three coyotes can sound like a dozen. Each one slides its pitch around while it howls, so a small family throws up a wall of voices — biologists call it the 'beau geste' effect.
coyote.hint: A den bank tucked into brushy cover, wide grass full of rabbits and voles, and water within reach. It only settles where there is already plenty to eat.
coyote.name: Coyote
coyote.preferredHabitat: Open grassland and edges with brushy cover for a den and water within reach
coyote.role: The animal at the top of this meadow, and the most adaptable carnivore in here. It hunts voles and rabbits alone, fawns in pairs, and eats fruit, insects and carrion in between. Its return is what finally puts pressure on the foxes, badgers and deer that nothing else here could touch — and it will happily trail a digging badger to snap up whatever bolts out the far side.
coyote.shelter: Raises pups in a den dug into a brushy bank, often an enlarged badger or fox burrow

crayfish.diet: decaying plants and carcasses, live aquatic plants, snails, insect larvae and freshwater shrimp.
crayfish.fact: Lose a claw in a fight and a crayfish just grows a new one, a little bigger at every moult, until it matches the old one. Startle it and it flips its tail and rockets backwards faster than you can grab.
crayfish.hint: A soft bank to tunnel into, sunken wood to hide under, and plenty of rotting plants to eat.
crayfish.name: Crayfish
crayfish.preferredHabitat: Slow, weedy water with woody cover and a bank soft enough to dig into.
crayfish.role: The marsh's recycler, and very nearly everybody's dinner. Crayfish shred dead plants and tidy up carcasses, turning buried gunk back into living meat — which the otter, the mink, the kingfisher, the merganser, the crane, the snapping turtle and the heron then come and take.
crayfish.shelter: Burrows dug into saturated banks, and gaps beneath sunken logs and stones.

crow.diet: crabs, shellfish, eggs, insects, fruit and whatever the tide leaves behind
crow.fact: Crows work out that a shell will break if you drop it on rock, and they pick their spot — one that has learned the trick will carry a clam up, drop it, and adjust its height until the shell cracks. They also remember faces for years.
crow.hint: A tall tree back from the beach to nest in, and a wrack line worth patrolling. It will find everything else on its own.
crow.name: Crow
crow.preferredHabitat: The strip where the beach meets the trees, with a clear view of the tideline
crow.role: The sharpest bird on the shore. It patrols the tideline for anything stranded, cracks open what it can't bite through, and follows the gulls and the otters to see what they turn up.
crow.shelter: A bulky stick nest high in a shore pine, reused and repaired year after year

desert-hawk.diet: jackrabbits, ground squirrels, quail, woodrats and lizards
desert-hawk.fact: These are the only birds of prey in the world that hunt in packs: a family of five or six spreads out, some crashing into a thorn bush to panic a rabbit while the others wait on the far side. And when there is nowhere decent to perch, they simply stand on each other's backs, three hawks high.
desert-hawk.hint: One bird is never the whole story. A family needs a tall cactus strong enough to hold the nest, high lookouts all around it, and open ground with rabbits crossing it.
desert-hawk.name: Desert Hawk
desert-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open scrub with tall cactus and trees to nest and keep lookout from
desert-hawk.role: The daytime top predator, working the same desert the mountain lion works at night. Two or three generations live together all year, share every kill, help feed each other's chicks and take turns on lookout — teamwork that lets them bring down jackrabbits far heavier than any single hawk. They need tall lookouts above open ground and a big cactus solid enough to hold a family nest.
desert-hawk.shelter: A bulky stick nest wedged in the arms of a tall cactus or a thorny tree, built and guarded by the whole family

desert-hummingbird.diet: nectar from chuparosa, ocotillo and creosote flowers, plus small insects and spiders
desert-hummingbird.fact: The male dives past the female at full speed and shrieks — except the shriek comes from his tail feathers, not his throat — while flaring a violet moustache of feathers out sideways.
desert-hummingbird.hint: Real flowers beat a feeder every time: chuparosa blooms right through the desert winter, and ocotillo takes over in spring.
desert-hummingbird.name: Desert Hummingbird
desert-hummingbird.preferredHabitat: Washes and flats with shrubs that flower in winter and spring
desert-hummingbird.role: A nectar-drinker that chases the bloom, arriving with the winter flowers of chuparosa and moving on as the desert dries out. It never needs to find water, and on the hardest days it switches itself almost off, dropping into a torpor so deep it feels cold to the touch.
desert-hummingbird.shelter: A thimble-sized cup of plant down and spider silk in a low shrub

desert-millipede.diet: dead leaves, stems, seed husks and other dry plant litter on the ground
desert-millipede.fact: A desert millipede spends most of the year underground, then comes pouring out by the hundreds after the first summer storm — and if you touch one it coils into a tight spiral like a cinnamon bun and oozes a bitter brown liquid that stains your fingers for days.
desert-millipede.hint: Let the leaves drift up under the shrubs and leave a slab it can crawl beneath. Damp litter is both its dinner and its hiding place — bare hot sand is neither.
desert-millipede.name: Desert Millipede
desert-millipede.preferredHabitat: Litter drifts under shrubs with rock slabs and diggable soil nearby
desert-millipede.role: The litter shredder. It chews dead leaves, stems and husks into crumbs small enough for termites and soil microbes to finish, which is how dead plants become soil again out here. It has hundreds of legs and absolutely no hurry — armour and a foul chemical mean it can afford to stroll — but scorpions and roadrunners eat it anyway.
desert-millipede.shelter: Buried in soil and tucked under litter and rock slabs by day; out walking on damp nights

desert-tarantula.diet: crickets, beetles, grasshoppers, termites and other spiders
desert-tarantula.fact: A frightened desert tarantula rubs its back legs over its belly and flicks off a cloud of barbed hairs that itch like fibreglass — and if nothing comes past to eat, it can simply wait, going a whole year between meals.
desert-tarantula.hint: Firm ground it can line with silk, and then quiet. A burrow it digs is one she may still be sitting in twenty years from now.
desert-tarantula.name: Desert Tarantula
desert-tarantula.preferredHabitat: Firm open ground between shrubs with litter and cover close by
desert-tarantula.role: A patient ambush hunter that lives at the mouth of a silk-lined burrow, feeling for the twitch of a cricket on the trip-lines at its door. A female may keep the same hole for twenty years, which makes her one of the longest-lived animals in the biome. Roadrunners take them — and so does the giant hairy scorpion, which outweighs a desert tarantula and is not remotely afraid of one.
desert-tarantula.shelter: A silk-lined burrow in firm soil, its doorway strung with trip-lines

desert-termite.diet: dead grass, fallen leaves, dry dung and the weathered outsides of dead wood
desert-termite.fact: These termites plaster a thin mud roof over a dead stem and eat underneath it, so they can feed in full sun without ever touching the dry air.
desert-termite.hint: Bury a little dead wood and they will find it — dead wood is the desert’s pantry.
desert-termite.name: Desert Termite
desert-termite.preferredHabitat: Soil beneath shrubs and grasses where dead plant litter collects
desert-termite.role: The animal that actually recycles this desert. There is too little water here for litter to rot the way it does in a forest, so termites eat almost all of it instead, carrying the nitrogen and carbon back underground and leaving tunnels that let rain soak in rather than run off. On swarm nights, everything with a beak or a sting comes to the feast.
desert-termite.shelter: Tunnels and chambers underground, plus mud sheeting built over whatever it is eating

desert-tortoise.diet: native grasses, spring wildflowers, and cactus pads and fruit
desert-tortoise.fact: A desert tortoise can live 80 years and spends about 95 of every 100 days of it underground — and it carries a bladder of stored water it can live off for a year if the rains fail.
desert-tortoise.hint: A caliche den on a rocky slope, with grass and wildflowers to graze in front of it. It drinks only when rain puddles, and can wait a whole year for that.
desert-tortoise.name: Desert Tortoise
desert-tortoise.preferredHabitat: Rocky slopes with native grasses and wildflowers
desert-tortoise.role: A slow, long-lived grazer that also happens to be the landlord. The dens it hollows out get used for years afterwards by owls, snakes, lizards, rodents and insects that could never dig anything like them, so saving one tortoise quietly saves a dozen other animals. Grown tortoises are nearly untouchable; it is the hatchlings, soft-shelled for years, that ravens and coyotes take.
desert-tortoise.shelter: Caliche caves, rock crevices and dens under boulders on rocky slopes

dragonfly.diet: flying insects as an adult; the underwater nymph takes midge larvae, freshwater shrimp, tadpoles and fish fry
dragonfly.fact: Dragonflies catch about 95 out of every 100 things they chase — a better strike rate than a lion, a shark or a falcon. They also see the world in something close to slow motion, which is why swatting one never works.
dragonfly.hint: Open, clean water for the nymphs below, and tall stems at the edge for them to climb when it is time to change.
dragonfly.name: Dragonfly
dragonfly.preferredHabitat: Clean open water with emergent stems to climb out on
dragonfly.role: A hunter with two completely different lives. The nymph spends a year underwater firing out a hinged, grabbing lower lip at tadpoles and fish fry; then it climbs a reed stem, splits its own back open and flies away to hunt mosquitoes over the marsh.
dragonfly.shelter: Emergent reed stems for the adults; the nymphs live in the water below

elf-owl.fact: The smallest owl in the world weighs about as much as a golf ball, and it nips the stinger off a scorpion before carrying the rest home to its chicks.
elf-owl.hint: Cactus alone will not do. A woodpecker has to drill the hole first and let the plant seal it into a boot.
elf-owl.name: Elf Owl
elf-owl.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands and mesquite washes full of old woodpecker holes
elf-owl.role: A migratory night hunter of moths and scorpions that cannot make a hole to save its life. Every nest it has ever used was chiselled out by a woodpecker and then hardened by the cactus into a waterproof boot. Plant a whole forest of cactus and you still get no elf owls until the woodpecker has done its work.
elf-owl.shelter: Old woodpecker holes in cactus and desert trees; it cannot carve its own

elk.diet: grass and leafy plants through the growing season; twigs, buds, bark and acorns once the green is gone
elk.fact: A bull elk grows a whole new set of antlers every year, laying down up to an inch of bone a day — the fastest-growing bone of any animal — and drops the lot each spring. In autumn he bugles: a squeal that carries more than a mile from an animal the size of a horse.
elk.hint: Grassy gaps and young regrowth to graze, thick cover to rest in, and a muddy wallow to roll in — a bull plasters himself in mud before he starts bugling.
elk.name: Elk
elk.preferredHabitat: Big blocks of forest broken by clearings and young regrowth to graze, thick cover to rest in, and a muddy wallow within a day's walk
elk.role: The elk is this forest's big grazer, and the only animal here that eats grass in bulk. Where a squirrel nibbles and a porcupine peels bark, a herd of elk crops whole clearings, keeping gaps open and sunlit so the plants and insects of the forest edge have somewhere to live — and grazing them bare if there are too many. Elk churn wallows into muddy pools that frogs and insects then breed in, carry seeds in their coats and droppings, and their calves are one of the few big meals a bear can find in spring. Elk vanished from these woods for more than a century and are back only where people put them back.
elk.shelter: No den — beds down in thick conifer cover by day and moves out into open gaps to feed at dawn and dusk

ermine.diet: small rodents, especially voles; also young pikas, birds, eggs and insects
ermine.fact: An ermine turns pure white in winter except for the black tip of its tail, and it is narrow enough to chase a vole down the vole's own tunnel.
ermine.hint: It moves into a burrow it has just emptied, so bring the small rodents back first.
ermine.name: Ermine
ermine.preferredHabitat: Talus and heath edges beside turf with dense rodent prey, used all year round
ermine.role: A weasel shaped like a furry pencil, living mostly on voles and mice and taking young pikas, nestlings and eggs besides. It builds nothing. It moves into the burrow of whatever it has just eaten and lines the nest with the previous owner's fur. It is here in every season, not only in the snow. Foxes, martens and eagles kill it in turn.
ermine.shelter: Dens taken over from its prey — rodent burrows and rock crevices, relined with the previous owner's fur

fisher.diet: small and medium mammals — porcupines, squirrels, hares — plus birds, carrion and fruit
fisher.fact: The fisher is one of the only animals that eats porcupines. It circles round to the face — the one place with no quills — and keeps biting until it can flip the porcupine over and reach the belly.
fisher.hint: Closed canopy overhead, a big living tree hollow enough to raise kits high off the ground, and squirrels and porcupines below to hunt.
fisher.name: Fisher
fisher.preferredHabitat: Unbroken conifer and mixed forest with a closed canopy and large hollow trees
fisher.role: The fisher treats the treetops like the ground, chasing squirrels through branches and catching flying squirrels most predators never even see, and it is the main check on porcupine numbers. Because it needs canopy that connects tree to tree and big trees hollow enough to raise kits inside, finding a fisher tells you the forest is old and joined up rather than cut into patches.
fisher.shelter: Dens in hollow logs and ground burrows; kits are raised in a cavity high inside a living tree

flying-squirrel.diet: mostly underground truffle fungi; also lichens, acorns, tree seeds and some insects
flying-squirrel.fact: Flying squirrels do not fly, they glide — and under ultraviolet light their fur glows bubblegum pink, something nobody noticed until a researcher pointed a UV torch into the trees a few years ago.
flying-squirrel.hint: Truffles in the soil to dig up and an old woodpecker hole to sleep in. It makes neither for itself.
flying-squirrel.name: Flying Squirrel
flying-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Cool, closed-canopy hemlock and hardwood forest with old cavity trees and a deep fungal layer in the soil
flying-squirrel.role: This squirrel lives mostly on mushrooms, and mostly on underground ones it has to smell through the soil and dig up. The spores ride through it and get planted at the next set of tree roots, so squirrel, fungus and tree are one loop that keeps all three going. It cannot cut a hole either, so it sleeps in old woodpecker cavities, huddled in a heap with others for warmth — and it is the favourite meal of owls and fishers, which is how energy from the underground fungi ends up at the very top of the food web.
flying-squirrel.shelter: Old woodpecker cavities and natural hollows; huddles in groups through winter to stay warm

forest-salamander.diet: small invertebrates: mites, springtails, spiders, beetles, ants and earthworms
forest-salamander.fact: Add up all the red-backed salamanders in a patch of forest and they can outweigh every bird in it. They have no lungs at all — the whole animal breathes through its skin.
forest-salamander.hint: This one skips the tadpole stage completely — the eggs hatch fully formed inside a rotting log. No pond needed, just damp wood and deep leaves.
forest-salamander.name: Forest Salamander
forest-salamander.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp deciduous forest floor with abundant rotting wood — and no pond required anywhere in its life
forest-salamander.role: This salamander is the bridge between the leaf litter and everything above it: it eats the mites, springtails and small worms that shred fallen leaves, and its own huge numbers feed snakes, birds and small mammals. It also breaks the rule everyone learns about amphibians — no pond, no tadpole, the entire life cycle inside one rotting log. Skin-breathing means it dries out fast, so the ground has to stay damp.
forest-salamander.shelter: Under logs, bark and damp leaf litter; lays its eggs in a cavity inside rotting wood and stays coiled around them

freshwater-mussel.diet: algae, bacteria and fine dead particles strained out of the water.
freshwater-mussel.fact: A baby mussel has to hitchhike. It clamps onto the gills of a passing fish and rides there for weeks before dropping off to start life on the bottom — and some mother mussels wave a flap of flesh shaped like a little fish to lure a host in close.
freshwater-mussel.hint: A settled bed that stays put for years — and fish, because young they ride to their new home clamped to fish gills.
freshwater-mussel.name: Freshwater Mussel
freshwater-mussel.preferredHabitat: Slow, settled water over firm silt and fine sand.
freshwater-mussel.role: The marsh's water filter, and one of the longest-lived animals in it. One mussel can strain the same patch of water for thirty years, dropping what it catches to the bottom for shrimp and crayfish. No fish means no baby mussels, so the mussels only come back after the minnows do.
freshwater-mussel.shelter: Burrowed upright in stable fine sediment with only its two siphons showing.

freshwater-shrimp.diet: dead leaves and stems, the fungi and bacteria growing on them, and algal film scraped off plants.
freshwater-shrimp.fact: Freshwater shrimp swim on their sides, and males carry females around piggyback for days before they mate. Lift a handful of soggy leaves out of a pond and dozens of them will be flicking about in it.
freshwater-shrimp.hint: A drift of rotting leaves in still water is all they need.
freshwater-shrimp.name: Freshwater Shrimp
freshwater-shrimp.preferredHabitat: Shallow, well-oxygenated water with a deep drift of decaying plant litter.
freshwater-shrimp.role: The marsh's shredder. One shrimp chews a single dead cattail leaf into thousands of crumbs — and it is really after the fungus furring the leaf, not the leaf itself. That is how a heap of dead plants becomes food for minnows, salamander larvae and dragonfly nymphs.
freshwater-shrimp.shelter: Among submerged litter, plant stems and the loose top layer of sediment.

garden-spider.diet: flying and jumping insects caught in the web — grasshoppers, bees, flies, moths
garden-spider.fact: This spider takes down most of its web every night and eats the old silk to build the next one — and it stitches a bold white zigzag through the middle that nobody has fully explained yet.
garden-spider.hint: Tall stiff stems left standing, spaced far enough apart to sling a big web between them, with flowers close by to bring the insects in.
garden-spider.name: Garden Spider
garden-spider.preferredHabitat: Sunny meadow with tall stiff vegetation left standing and plenty of flying insects
garden-spider.role: The meadow's trapper. It slings a wheel of silk wider than your hand between tall stems and waits head-down at the hub for grasshoppers, bees and flies to blunder in. Spiders are the largest predator group in any grassland and the biggest single thing missing from this meadow until now — they eat enormous numbers of insects, and they are in turn the main food of half the songbirds here.
garden-spider.shelter: Hangs head-down at the hub of its own orb web, slung between tall standing stems

garter-snake.diet: earthworms, pillbugs, amphibians, slugs, insects and young rodents
garter-snake.fact: Garter snakes spend the whole winter piled together by the dozen in one frost-free hole underground, and come pouring back out of it in a knot in spring.
garter-snake.hint: Water to hunt beside, warm stone to bask on, and a den deep enough to spend the winter below the frost.
garter-snake.name: Garter Snake
garter-snake.preferredHabitat: Moist meadow and grassland near sunny stones and water
garter-snake.role: The meadow's damp-grass hunter — earthworms, pillbugs, frogs, insects and young voles, always within reach of water. It is harmless to people, though a bite can itch. Where it can survive the winter is what decides where it can live at all, so one deep frost-free den matters more than anything else you can build for it.
garter-snake.shelter: Shelters under stone walls and logs; winters below the frost line in a communal den

golden-eagle.diet: marmots, hares, ground squirrels, white-tailed ptarmigan and other birds, plus carrion
golden-eagle.fact: A hunting golden eagle drops out of the sky at over 240 kilometres an hour, and its eyesight is sharp enough to pick a yellow-bellied marmot out of a boulder field from a kilometre up.
golden-eagle.hint: This one comes last, when the mountain is properly alive again. It needs a real cliff for the eyrie and open ground below with plenty moving on it.
golden-eagle.name: Golden Eagle
golden-eagle.preferredHabitat: Open, high country with big cliffs to nest on and plenty of medium-sized prey
golden-eagle.role: The hunter that owns the air up here, taking marmots, hares and white-tailed ptarmigan in long stooping dives and killing smaller predators outright when it gets the chance. It takes newborn lambs, kids and fox cubs, but not adult sheep or goats. Its huge stick eyrie on a cliff ledge gets added to and reused for decades. Adults have nothing above them.
golden-eagle.shelter: Huge stick eyries built on sheer cliff ledges and reused for decades

goshawk.diet: squirrels, jays, grouse, rabbits and woodpeckers, chased down inside the trees
goshawk.fact: A goshawk hunts by crashing straight through the branches at full speed with its wings half folded, and it will dive at anything — including people — that walks too near its nest.
goshawk.hint: Grow the forest tall and leave the understory open. It needs a big limb to nest on and room to fly hard between the trunks.
goshawk.name: Goshawk
goshawk.preferredHabitat: Mature forest with a high closed canopy and open flying room underneath it
goshawk.role: The goshawk is the forest's top daytime hunter and the reason squirrels freeze against tree trunks. Short broad wings and a long steering tail let it turn inside a wood at speed, so unlike a soaring hawk it hunts under the canopy rather than above it. It needs old forest with big limbs to nest on and clear space beneath to fly, which makes its arrival a sign that the trees have finally grown up.
goshawk.shelter: A broad stick nest built against the trunk on a heavy limb, halfway up a big old tree in closed canopy

grasshopper.fact: A grasshopper's ears are on its belly — a pair of eardrums on the first segment of the abdomen, nowhere near its head.
grasshopper.hint: They return almost as soon as the grass does.
grasshopper.name: Grasshopper
grasshopper.preferredHabitat: Sunny grasslands and meadows rich in grasses and forbs
grasshopper.role: Grasshoppers turn grass into food for everything else. Almost every meat-eater in this meadow takes them at some point — birds, snakes, foxes, spiders, mantises, even a screech owl — so a good grasshopper summer is a good summer for the whole food web.
grasshopper.shelter: Shelters down in grass and low vegetation; lays eggs in firm bare soil

grasshopper-mouse.diet: scorpions, centipedes, beetles and other mice
grasshopper-mouse.fact: This mouse hunts scorpions, gets stung in the face, and carries on eating — its body turns the venom's pain signal off. Then it stands up on its hind legs and howls at the moon like a tiny wolf.
grasshopper-mouse.hint: An old burrow it can take over and open ground to hunt across. It gets all its water from what it catches.
grasshopper-mouse.name: Grasshopper Mouse
grasshopper-mouse.preferredHabitat: Open sandy flats with scattered brush and plenty of prey underfoot
grasshopper-mouse.role: A mouse that decided to be a predator. It keeps scorpions and big insects in check, and it is one of the only animals that can eat the desert's most venomous residents without flinching.
grasshopper-mouse.shelter: Takes over a burrow another animal dug, then defends it

gray-crowned-rosy-finch.diet: tiny alpine plant seeds and insects, often gleaned off the surface of snowfields
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.fact: It nests higher than almost any other songbird here, jammed into cracks in cliffs and rockslides where nothing else will build at all.
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.hint: Rock with cracks in it, not a heap of stones. This one nests inside the cliff, feeds out across the scree, and drinks meltwater.
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.name: Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.preferredHabitat: Above treeline: talus, scree, cliff faces and the edges of permanent snow
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.role: A pink-brown finch that hops across snowfields picking up wind-blown seeds and insects the cold has knocked flat. It can only breed where the rock has real cracks in it, so cliffs matter to it even more than food does. Eagles and ermines take it.
gray-crowned-rosy-finch.shelter: Bulky cup of moss and grass wedged deep into a cliff crack or a hole in talus

gray-fox.diet: mice, voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds and eggs — and in late summer an astonishing amount of fruit
gray-fox.fact: It is the only dog in the world that climbs trees. A gray fox hooks its curved claws into the bark, shins up the trunk like a cat, and naps ten metres up where nothing that hunts it can follow.
gray-fox.hint: A brushy edge to hunt along, a dry bank to den in, and something woody to climb — going straight up a trunk is how this one gets away from whatever is bigger. Fruit matters as much as mice here.
gray-fox.name: Gray Fox
gray-fox.preferredHabitat: Brushy woodland edges and old clearings growing back, with tangled climbable cover
gray-fox.role: The forest's climbing fox. It works the brushy edges for mice, rabbits and ground-nesting birds, then goes straight up a trunk after squirrels, nests and grapes. By late summer it is eating so much fruit that its droppings are half seeds, which plants the next generation of berry tangles all along the edge. Bobcats kill it when they catch it in the open and great horned owls take its kits, so it keeps a climbable tree within a sprint at all times.
gray-fox.shelter: Hollow logs, rock crevices and old earth dens; it will also curl up on a branch well off the ground

gray-whale.diet: bottom-living amphipods and swarming mysid shrimp, sifted through baleen
gray-whale.fact: Gray whales roll onto one side and vacuum the seafloor, straining out shrimp-like amphipods and leaving long muddy plumes trailing behind them — and they do it at the end of a swim of up to 14,000 miles.
gray-whale.hint: Give this one deep water and a seabed thick with tiny shrimp-like amphipods. Tidepools and dune plantings will never bring it in.
gray-whale.name: Gray Whale
gray-whale.preferredHabitat: Nearshore water with soft-bottom freshwater shrimp beds and mysid swarms at the kelp edge
gray-whale.role: A baleen whale that feeds off the bottom rather than skimming the surface, so a whale that lingers offshore is really a report on the seabed and the kelp edge below it. Adults are far too big to be hunted here; the calves travelling with them in spring are not, and orcas know it.
gray-whale.shelter: Open ocean; passes close inshore along a healthy coast

great-blue-heron.diet: fish, frogs, salamanders, crayfish and large insects
great-blue-heron.fact: A heron's neck has one specially kinked bone in it that works like a loaded spring — the strike is over faster than you can blink, and the fish is caught crosswise in the bill rather than speared.
great-blue-heron.hint: Shallow water full of fish and frogs, and a stand of tall trees for the colony. This one nests alongside its own kind or not at all.
great-blue-heron.name: Great Blue Heron
great-blue-heron.preferredHabitat: Still shallows for slow, patient hunting, with tall nest trees within reach
great-blue-heron.role: The tall grey statue of the shallows. It hunts alone but flatly refuses to nest alone, packing dozens of stick nests into one stand of tall trees — and it spends a good part of its life being chased and robbed of its catch by eagles.
great-blue-heron.shelter: Colonial stick nests built high in tall trees and snags near water

great-horned-owl.diet: mammals and birds — rabbits, skunks, even other owls — plus frogs
great-horned-owl.fact: Great horned owls are one of the only animals that regularly kill and eat skunks. The spray does not appear to bother them in the slightest.
great-horned-owl.hint: Tall trees holding somebody else's old nest — this one never builds its own — and prey already back in the woods.
great-horned-owl.name: Great Horned Owl
great-horned-owl.preferredHabitat: Mature forest broken by open ground, with big trees holding other animals' abandoned nests
great-horned-owl.role: The great horned owl runs the night shift and eats a longer list of animals than any other bird of prey here — squirrels, bats, snakes, ducks, even porcupines — and adults have nothing above them. It builds nothing at all: it starts nesting in midwinter by claiming an old squirrel drey or hawk nest somebody else made last spring, which is why the squirrels have to come back before the owl can.
great-horned-owl.shelter: Never builds a nest: takes over an old hawk, crow or squirrel nest, or a broken snag top or ledge

grizzly-bear.diet: roots and berries dug out of the slope, ground squirrels and marmots, winter-killed carcasses — and moths, by the hundred thousand
grizzly-bear.fact: Grizzlies climb above the trees in late summer to eat moths — flipping rocks to get at them and putting away up to 40,000 in a day, which is most of a year's fat in a few weeks.
grizzly-bear.hint: A high open slope soft enough to dig, rocks to flip for moths, and a mountain already full enough to feed something this big.
grizzly-bear.name: Grizzly Bear
grizzly-bear.preferredHabitat: Open high country with digging ground, berry slopes and no people
grizzly-bear.role: The biggest thing on the mountain and the reason everything else stays alert. It digs whole slopes apart for roots and ground squirrels, which turns the soil over, and in late summer it climbs above the trees to eat moths off the rockslides. It will drive a wolverine off a carcass without breaking stride.
grizzly-bear.shelter: Digs a den into a high slope in autumn and sleeps in it until the snow softens

ground-squirrel.diet: mostly seeds, grasses, flowers and fungi, plus insects like grasshoppers
ground-squirrel.fact: Facing a rattlesnake, this squirrel kicks sand and waves its tail — and pumps hot blood into the tail first, so the snake's heat-sensing pits see a far bigger animal than is really standing there.
ground-squirrel.hint: Deep diggable soil for a burrow town, and a stone wall to stand sentry on.
ground-squirrel.name: Ground Squirrel
ground-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Open grassy meadow and slopes with a stone wall or bank to keep watch from
ground-squirrel.role: A digger and a generalist. It eats seeds, greens, fungi and insects, turns over soil every time it excavates, and the tunnels it abandons become homes for bumble bee queens, garter snakes and foxes. Its colonies are what pull badgers, hawks and coyotes into a meadow in the first place.
ground-squirrel.shelter: Big multi-entrance burrow systems dug into deep open ground

groundhog.diet: grass, clover, dandelions and just about any tender green thing it can reach
groundhog.fact: A groundhog digs a burrow with a front door, a back door, a bedroom and a separate room for going to the toilet — and moves about a tonne of soil doing it. In winter its heart slows to about five beats a minute.
groundhog.hint: Deep, well-drained soil at the edge of the grass, with a bolt-hole close by. It wants somewhere to dig more than somewhere to hide.
groundhog.name: Groundhog
groundhog.preferredHabitat: Meadow edges with deep, well-drained soil it can tunnel through
groundhog.role: The meadow's earthmover. Its abandoned burrows become homes for foxes, snakes, rabbits and half the small animals here, so one groundhog's digging outlives the groundhog by years.
groundhog.shelter: A burrow with several entrances, a grass-lined sleeping chamber and a separate toilet room

gull.diet: fish, crabs, mussels, sea stars and carrion
gull.fact: A gull that finds a mussel it cannot open carries it high into the air and drops it onto rock — and it remembers which rock cracks shells best, coming back to the same one all season.
gull.hint: Open beach to patrol, low scrub to nest beside, and one hard flat rock to bomb shellfish onto.
gull.name: Gull
gull.preferredHabitat: Any shoreline with food to scavenge or catch
gull.role: A bold, clever generalist that scavenges carrion and hunts crabs, shellfish, anchovies and even sea stars, tying dozens of small animals to the top of the food web. Nothing on this shore hunts a grown gull, which is exactly why it can afford to be so cheeky.
gull.shelter: Ground scrapes on offshore rocks and islands, tucked beside driftwood, rock or low coastal scrub

harbor-seal.diet: fish, especially anchovy and flatfish, plus squid, octopus and crustaceans
harbor-seal.fact: Harbor seals can sleep at sea, hanging upright just below the surface like bottles and bobbing up for a breath without properly waking.
harbor-seal.hint: Deep water to fish in and quiet rocks to haul out on, with room around them. A haul-out is not a bird nesting closure — build the right thing.
harbor-seal.name: Harbor Seal
harbor-seal.preferredHabitat: Calm, clean water beside a haul-out nobody walks up to
harbor-seal.role: A patient, curious hunter that eats whatever fish is easiest to catch that week. Everything it does on land happens on a haul-out: resting, moulting, giving birth. Walk up to one once and the seals stop using it. Nothing on this shore hunts an adult seal — but something out in the deep water does.
harbor-seal.shelter: Undisturbed low-tide rocks and sandbars used as haul-outs for resting and pupping
