hermit-crab.fact: Hermit crabs queue up by size and swap houses in a chain: the biggest one moves into the new shell, the next takes the house it left, and so on all the way down the line until the smallest crab gets an upgrade.
hermit-crab.hint: A pool is not enough. Leave a supply of empty snail shells, or there is nothing to move into.
hermit-crab.name: Hermit Crab
hermit-crab.preferredHabitat: Tidepools and low rock benches with a supply of empty snail shells
hermit-crab.role: A tidepool tidier that grazes algae and cleans up dead things — and one of the shore's great recyclers, since every shell it wears is the leftover of a snail. What limits hermit crabs is almost never food. It is houses.

horned-lizard.diet: harvester ants above all — about nine mouthfuls in ten — plus termites and a few other insects
horned-lizard.fact: Cornered, a horned lizard squirts a jet of its own blood out of the corners of its eyes — it can carry a metre — and it tastes so foul that a fox will spit and keep spitting for minutes.
horned-lizard.hint: No ants, nothing doing. Leave the gaps between the shrubs bare and open — that is exactly where harvester ants clear their mounds.
horned-lizard.name: Horned Lizard
horned-lizard.preferredHabitat: Open sandy ground between shrubs, near harvester ant mounds
horned-lizard.role: An ant specialist with a stomach far too big for its body, because harvester ants are such poor food that it has to eat hundreds every day just to break even. Those ants only build on open bare ground, so the tidier, greener and more trampled a desert gets, the faster this flat little lizard vanishes from it.
horned-lizard.shelter: Shuffles itself down into loose sand; shelters under low shrubs

jackrabbit.diet: grasses, wildflowers, cactus pads, and the twigs and bark of desert shrubs
jackrabbit.fact: Those enormous ears are radiators — a jackrabbit lies dead still in the shade and pours its body heat straight out through the blood vessels inside them.
jackrabbit.hint: Grass to graze, shrubs to browse and a shaded scrape to lie in. Skip the water — it drinks from the plants.
jackrabbit.name: Jackrabbit
jackrabbit.preferredHabitat: Open flats with scattered shrubs and room to run
jackrabbit.role: The biggest everyday plant-eater here, and the meal at the centre of everyone else's day. Its babies are born furred and open-eyed in a shallow scrape, because a jackrabbit owns no burrow and never will — it bets everything on ears, speed and knowing where the shade is.
jackrabbit.shelter: A shallow shaded scrape under a shrub; it never digs a burrow

javelina.diet: prickly pear pads, mesquite pods, agave hearts, roots and tubers
javelina.fact: A javelina eats prickly pear whole — spines and all — and has a scent gland on its back so strong that a herd can find each other in the dark by smell alone.
javelina.hint: Grow the prickly pear and leave a shaded thorny tangle to bed down in. A herd sleeps out the middle of the day and feeds at dusk.
javelina.name: Javelina
javelina.preferredHabitat: Desert scrub and washes with thick thorny cover and stands of prickly pear
javelina.role: Javelinas are the desert's cactus processors: they crunch through pads that nothing else will touch, which keeps prickly pear from taking over a wash and spreads its seeds in their droppings. Rooting for tubers turns over hard-crusted soil and buries litter, giving seeds somewhere to germinate after rain. They travel in herds of six to a dozen, and the herd smell is also the alarm system, because their eyesight is terrible.
javelina.shelter: Beds down as a herd in the shade of dense thornscrub or a rock overhang through the heat of the day

kangaroo-rat.diet: seeds, carried home in fur-lined cheek pouches and buried in underground larders
kangaroo-rat.fact: A kangaroo rat never drinks — it manufactures all the water it needs out of dry seeds — and it can leap sideways almost two metres to dodge a striking snake.
kangaroo-rat.hint: Seed plants and soft diggable soil, especially the loose mounds heaped round a shrub's base. Build no water at all — this one may never take a drink in its life.
kangaroo-rat.name: Kangaroo Rat
kangaroo-rat.preferredHabitat: Loose soil under seed-bearing shrubs and mesquite
kangaroo-rat.role: The desert's accidental gardener. It buries seeds all over its patch and forgets enough of them that those are the plants that come up next spring. Its tunnels are the starting point for everything that cannot dig well: kit foxes widen them into dens, and half the burrows in the biome began as its work. Nearly every predator here eats it.
kangaroo-rat.shelter: Shallow burrows under shrubs and soil mounds, plugged with sand every dawn

kingfisher.fact: A kingfisher shuts its eyes just before it hits the water, so the last part of the dive is flown blind from memory. Then it whacks the fish against a branch and swallows it head-first so the fins fold the right way.
kingfisher.hint: Clear open water to dive into and a bare vertical earth bank to tunnel into. A nest box is no use to a bird that digs its own.
kingfisher.name: Kingfisher
kingfisher.preferredHabitat: Clear water with a bare vertical bank beside it and perches overhead
kingfisher.role: The rattling plunge-diver of the marsh, and one of the rare birds where the female is the flashier of the pair. It digs its own nest tunnel a metre back into a bare earth bank, so a marsh stuffed with fish but with no raw bank still gets no kingfishers.
kingfisher.shelter: Tunnel burrows dug a metre or more into bare earthen banks

kit-fox.diet: kangaroo rats and other rodents, jackrabbits, squirrels, lizards, insects and some fruit
kit-fox.fact: The smallest wild dog here weighs less than a house cat, and its ridiculous ears do two jobs at once: hearing a mouse move underground, and shedding body heat like radiators.
kit-fox.hint: Rodents first — its den is a borrowed burrow made bigger. It never needs a drink you provide.
kit-fox.name: Kit Fox
kit-fox.preferredHabitat: Open desert with loose soil and plenty of small prey
kit-fox.role: A night fox that lives almost entirely on rodents and hardly ever drinks — it takes its water out of what it catches. It rarely digs a den from scratch; it moves into a kangaroo rat's burrow and enlarges it, then keeps several doors open so a mountain lion can never corner it in there.
kit-fox.shelter: A cool underground den with several doors, usually a rodent burrow it has widened

ladybug.diet: aphids and other small soft-bodied insects, as both larva and adult
ladybug.fact: One ladybug can put away around 5,000 aphids in a lifetime. Pinch it and it bleeds bitter yellow blood out of its knees, which is why most birds spit it straight back out.
ladybug.hint: A patch of clover. The aphids arrive on their own, and that is the whole invitation.
ladybug.name: Ladybug
ladybug.preferredHabitat: Meadows with aphid-bearing plants, especially milkweed
ladybug.role: Larva and adult both hunt aphids, so a ladybug's whole life runs on an aphid supply — in this meadow, the yellow oleander aphids crowding the milkweed stems. Its bright shell is a warning label and it works on most birds. Mantises and orb weavers are not most birds.
ladybug.shelter: Overwinters packed into leaf litter in big huddles; shelters on foliage in summer

leopard-frog.diet: insects, spiders and worms taken in wet meadows and along the water's edge
leopard-frog.fact: A startled leopard frog leaps in zig-zags away from the water instead of towards it — and the second it lands in long grass those big dark spots break its outline up and it vanishes.
leopard-frog.hint: A lily pool to breed in and a wide band of damp meadow beside it to spend the whole summer hunting in.
leopard-frog.name: Leopard Frog
leopard-frog.preferredHabitat: Lily-fringed shallows with wet meadow beside them
leopard-frog.role: The frog that leaves the pond. It spends the whole summer hunting insects out in damp meadow and only hops back to the water in autumn, which is why a marsh mown right to the waterline loses its leopard frogs first.
leopard-frog.shelter: Shallow water in spring; damp grassy meadow through the summer

luna-moth.diet: hickory, walnut, sweetgum and birch leaves as a caterpillar; the adult eats nothing at all
luna-moth.fact: An adult luna moth has no mouth. It hatches out with about a week to live, never eats once, and spends the whole of it looking for a mate.
luna-moth.hint: Plant the leafy trees, then let the leaves lie where they fall. The cocoons spend the whole winter down in that litter.
luna-moth.name: Luna Moth
luna-moth.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous woodland with deep undisturbed leaf litter under the host trees
luna-moth.role: Luna moth caterpillars are leaf-eaters that turn tree leaves into fat, high-energy insect bodies, and everything from bats to jays cashes that in. The long twisted tails on the hindwings are an anti-bat device: they spin as the moth flies and throw a bat's echolocation off target, so the bat grabs a tail streamer instead of the body. Because the cocoon overwinters in fallen leaves, a forest that gets raked loses its luna moths even if every host tree is still standing.
luna-moth.shelter: A papery cocoon spun inside a curled leaf that falls to the ground, where it lies buried in the litter all winter

lynx.diet: snowshoe hares above all — sometimes almost nothing else — plus white-tailed ptarmigan, ground squirrels and young marmots
lynx.fact: A lynx weighs about as much as a border collie, but its paws are as wide as a mountain lion's. They spread as it steps, so it walks on top of snow a fox would sink straight through.
lynx.hint: No hares, nothing doing — it really is that simple. Get the dwarf-pine thickets back so hares have somewhere to hide, and it will move into a hollow under the rocks that something else dug.
lynx.name: Lynx
lynx.preferredHabitat: High snowy country with thickets of dwarf conifer where hares can hide and lynx can wait for them
lynx.role: The mountain's hare specialist, and almost nothing else will do. When hares are everywhere, lynx are everywhere; when the hares crash a few years later, the lynx crash right behind them, and the whole thing swings back and forth on roughly a ten-year beat. It hunts by sitting perfectly still in the thickets and letting the hare come to it, so low tangled cover matters more to it than open ground. It rarely digs, moving instead into a hollow under rock that somebody else opened up. Eagles take its kittens.
lynx.shelter: A hollow under boulders, roots or deadfall, often a burrow something else started and it widened

mallard.diet: mostly seeds and submerged plants, though hens switch to insect larvae, snails and freshwater shrimp while laying, and ducklings eat almost nothing else at first
mallard.fact: Mallards sleep with one eye open and half the brain awake. On a raft of sleeping ducks it is the ones on the outside doing the watching — and they swap places so everyone gets a proper nap.
mallard.hint: Water shallow enough to tip into headfirst, and thick dry tussocks a few steps up the bank for the hen to hide her nest in.
mallard.name: Mallard
mallard.preferredHabitat: Calm, plant-rich shallows with tussock cover on the bank
mallard.role: The tail-up dabbler of the shallows, tipping forward to reach seeds and leaves it can't dive for. Hens switch to insects and snails while they are laying, and ducklings eat almost nothing else at first, so a mallard family needs a bug-rich marsh, not just a weedy one.
mallard.shelter: Ground nests hidden in dense sedge and grass tussocks near water

marsh-wren.diet: insects and spiders picked from marsh stems
marsh-wren.fact: A male marsh wren builds up to a dozen empty practice nests for one female to come and inspect — and while he is at it he will sneak into a neighbour's nest and punch holes in the eggs.
marsh-wren.hint: Bulrush and cattail standing in water — stiff stems it can weave a hanging ball nest between.
marsh-wren.name: Marsh Wren
marsh-wren.preferredHabitat: Cattail and bulrush stands over water
marsh-wren.role: A thumb-sized bird with an enormous attitude. It runs up and down reed stems picking off spiders and insects, stitches hanging ball nests between the stiff stalks, and robs the eggs of anything that nests too close.
marsh-wren.shelter: Woven dome nests lashed among cattails and bulrushes

merganser.diet: small fish, crayfish, dragonfly nymphs and other aquatic insects
merganser.fact: Merganser ducklings jump out of a tree hole up to fifteen metres above the ground the day after they hatch, bounce off the leaf litter unhurt, and are diving for their own food within a day of landing.
merganser.hint: A wooded pond with dead trees still standing in it. The hen wants a hole in a drowned alder — a nest box is only a stand-in.
merganser.name: Merganser
merganser.preferredHabitat: Quiet ponds with drowned standing trees
merganser.role: A tiny diving duck with a fold-out white fan on its head, a saw-edged bill for gripping slippery fish, and a clear third eyelid it wears like swimming goggles. It nests in holes in drowned trees, which makes a beaver pond exactly its sort of place.
merganser.shelter: Tree cavities in standing dead timber over or beside water

mink.diet: fish, frogs, crayfish, muskrats, and the eggs and young of marsh birds
mink.fact: A mink will chase a fish thirty metres underwater, and it hunts on land, in the water and up trees. What it almost never does is dig — it simply moves into a burrow a muskrat made and does not ask.
mink.hint: Water to hunt in, and a bank den — but something else has to dig that den first.
mink.name: Mink
mink.role: A small brown fury with an enormous menu: fish, frogs, crayfish, muskrats, eggs, ducklings, whatever is slowest that day. Its home is always second-hand, so no muskrats usually means no mink no matter how much prey there is.
mink.shelter: Bank burrows, usually taken over from muskrats rather than dug

minnow.diet: algae, diatoms and plankton sifted off mud, stems and stones, plus detritus and small insect larvae.
minnow.fact: The male minnow scrubs the underside of a sunken slab spotless using a spongy pad on his own back, then guards the eggs the females glue to that ceiling — fanning them day and night until they hatch.
minnow.hint: Clean pools that join up to each other, plus something flat and submerged for the males to glue their eggs underneath.
minnow.name: Minnow
minnow.role: The little silver engine of the marsh. Minnow schools graze algae and plankton and then get eaten by nearly everything with a bill, a beak or a claw — and they give baby mussels a free ride to new water on their gills.
minnow.shelter: Reed roots, submerged plant beds, and the shaded underside of sunken wood.

monarch-butterfly.diet: caterpillars eat only milkweed; adults sip flower nectar
monarch-butterfly.fact: No single monarch flies the whole round trip. The butterflies that head south in autumn are the great-grandchildren of the ones that came north in spring, and they find the same groves anyway.
monarch-butterfly.hint: A spreading milkweed bed for the caterpillars — nothing else will do — and nectar flowers close by for the adults.
monarch-butterfly.name: Monarch Butterfly
monarch-butterfly.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and roadsides with milkweed to breed on and nectar flowers to refuel on
monarch-butterfly.role: Monarch caterpillars eat milkweed and store its poison in their own bodies, so a bird that tries one usually spits it out and remembers the orange for the rest of its life. It doesn't save them from everything — mantises, spiders, wasps and ants take eggs and caterpillars by the thousand, and only a few in every hundred ever grow wings.
monarch-butterfly.shelter: Roosts in trees and shrubs; overwinters clustered in dense groves far to the south

moose.diet: submerged pondweed and water lilies in summer, willow and aspen twigs in winter
moose.fact: A moose can hold its breath for a minute and walk along the bottom of a pond with its whole head underwater, pulling up plants by the roots.
moose.hint: Grow the underwater plant beds first and keep the water clear. It comes for what is growing under the surface, not on the bank.
moose.name: Moose
moose.preferredHabitat: Marsh and pond edge with deep willow thickets and clear shallow water full of submerged plants
moose.role: Moose come to the wetland for sodium, which the submerged plants have and the forest browse does not, and a big one can pull 20 kilograms of pondweed a day out of the shallows. That heavy grazing keeps open lanes through the plant beds where ducks feed and fish shelter, and the willow they browse in winter grows back thicker and lower — which is better cover for everything small. Their trails through the marsh become channels that hold water in dry summers.
moose.shelter: Beds pressed into willow thickets and shaded marsh edge; in summer it stands chest-deep in water to escape flies

mountain-chickadee.diet: insects, spiders and bark-beetle larvae in summer; cached conifer seeds in fall and winter
mountain-chickadee.fact: It hides thousands of seeds one at a time and remembers where they are. The part of its brain that does the remembering actually grows bigger in autumn.
mountain-chickadee.hint: Dead trees are the point. An old woodpecker hole is both shelter and a starting place — this one takes a ready-made cavity and works it wider. The whitebark pines come from its forgotten seeds.
mountain-chickadee.name: Mountain Chickadee
mountain-chickadee.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest of fir and whitebark pine with standing dead trees
mountain-chickadee.role: The small busy bird that seems to be everywhere in the last trees, hanging upside down off twigs after insects and beetle grubs and switching to hidden seeds in winter. It can only nest where the wood has already gone soft, so dead trees are not mess, they are the nursery. Weasels, foxes and martens take it.
mountain-chickadee.shelter: Existing cavities in dead conifers — old woodpecker holes, or soft rotten wood it can enlarge

mountain-goat.diet: grasses, sedges and alpine forbs in summer; lichen, moss and shrub twigs scraped off rock in winter
mountain-goat.fact: A mountain goat's hooves split apart as it steps, gripping stone like the rubber on climbing shoes, and it will sleep on a ledge no wider than a doormat with a 300-metre drop underneath it.
mountain-goat.hint: Steeper is better. Give it cliff ledges to bed on, turf to graze between them, and a mineral lick, because it will travel for hours to eat salty ground. Do not expect one out on the open flats.
mountain-goat.name: Mountain Goat
mountain-goat.preferredHabitat: The steepest broken cliff and ledge ground above the treeline, with turf to graze and a mineral seep within reach
mountain-goat.role: The white climber of the high cliffs, grazing turf and lichen and then retreating onto ground so steep that almost nothing can follow. That is the whole trick: goats live where other big grazers simply cannot go. They will walk for hours to a mineral lick and shove each other around at it. Mountain lions are the real threat, while eagles and wolverines take kids. In some ranges goats are native and in others people brought them in, so a white goat on a skyline is not always a local.
mountain-goat.shelter: Beds scraped out on narrow cliff ledges and in shallow caves under overhangs

mountain-lion.diet: deer and wild sheep mostly, plus jackrabbits, foxes and anything else it can get close enough to
mountain-lion.fact: The biggest cat out here cannot roar. It purrs like a house cat, screams like something out of a nightmare, and can jump five metres straight up onto a ledge from standing.
mountain-lion.hint: Big prey first, then rough broken ground to stalk through and a sheltered overhang for the kittens. Unlike most things out here it does come down to drink.
mountain-lion.name: Mountain Lion
mountain-lion.preferredHabitat: Broken canyon country with ledges, boulders and brush to stalk through, and somewhere reliable to drink
mountain-lion.role: The top of the desert food chain and a pure ambush hunter — it does not chase things down, it gets close and then explodes. Because it kills by stalking, it needs broken ground and brush to hide in; out on the open flat it goes hungry. It drags a big kill into cover and buries it under sticks and sand to come back to for days, which quietly feeds ravens, foxes and half the beetles in the wash. Kittens spend their first weeks tucked into a cave in a canyon wall, and nothing out here hunts a grown lion.
mountain-lion.shelter: No fixed home; the kittens are hidden in a dry cave or overhang in a canyon wall

mule-deer.diet: shrubs, forbs, twigs and buds, plus grasses in spring
mule-deer.fact: A bounding mule deer lands on all four hooves at once like a pogo stick, and puffs out scent from a gland on its hind leg as it goes — a warning the other deer can smell.
mule-deer.hint: Real browse — serviceberry twigs and buds, not lawn — plus water it can reach every day.
mule-deer.name: Mule Deer
mule-deer.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and shrubby edges with browse and daily water
mule-deer.role: The mule deer is a browser rather than a grazer: it works on shrub twigs, buds and broad-leaved plants instead of cropping turf, so it shapes the edges of the meadow rather than the middle. Its browsing and droppings move nutrients around. Coyotes take fawns; a healthy adult is more than most hunters here want to take on.
mule-deer.shelter: Beds down in brushy cover or tall grass; no permanent den

muskrat.diet: mainly cattails, bulrush and roots; sometimes freshwater mussels and small fish
muskrat.fact: A muskrat can stay under for a quarter of an hour on one breath, and in midwinter it dives beneath the ice to dig up frozen-in cattail roots and eat them down there in the dark.
muskrat.hint: Cattails to eat and to build lodges from, and shallow water over their roots so it can keep feeding all winter.
muskrat.name: Muskrat
muskrat.role: The cattail harvester. It clips reeds into lodges and feeding lanes that ducks and herons then hunt along, it feeds the mink, the otter and the eagle, and the bank burrows it abandons are the only homes mink ever move into.
muskrat.shelter: Dome lodges woven from cattail and reed, and burrows dug into banks

mussel.fact: A mussel glues itself to the rock with threads it spins out of its own foot — and if it does not like where it landed, it cuts them, crawls a little way, and glues itself down again.
mussel.hint: A filter feeder needs water that keeps moving. Give it surge-washed rock rather than a still pool, and barnacle crust for the young to settle on.
mussel.name: Mussel
mussel.preferredHabitat: Exposed rocky shore with clean, constantly moving water
mussel.role: A shellfish that builds its own reef. The beds pile up thick enough that hundreds of smaller animals live in the gaps between shells, and half this shore's hunters — sea stars, oystercatchers, turnstones, otters — are really just here for the mussels.
mussel.shelter: Dense beds anchored to wave-washed rock by byssal threads

nutcracker.diet: whitebark and limber pine seeds cached by the thousand, plus insects and small animals
nutcracker.fact: One bird buries tens of thousands of pine seeds in a single autumn and can still find them months later under snow, navigating by rocks and logs it has memorised like landmarks on a map.
nutcracker.hint: It needs a seed bank it can find again under the snow. Build the caches, and the pines it forgets to dig up become next year's forest.
nutcracker.name: Nutcracker
nutcracker.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest and krummholz within reach of pine-seed sources
nutcracker.role: A crow-family bird with a deal running with the whitebark pine. The cones never open by themselves, so nearly every young whitebark on the mountain grew from a seed this bird buried and never came back for. It carries seeds in a pouch under its tongue, breeds in late winter off its hoard, and takes insects and small animals besides. Martens and eagles catch it.
nutcracker.shelter: Cup nest in a conifer, sited near the winter seed caches

nuthatch.diet: insects and spiders from bark in summer; acorns, hickory nuts and cached seeds through winter
nuthatch.fact: A nuthatch walks down tree trunks head-first, which lets it spot insects tucked in bark that every upward-climbing bird walks straight past.
nuthatch.hint: An old woodpecker hole it can move straight into, with big oaks to work over and stash seeds in.
nuthatch.name: Nuthatch
nuthatch.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous and mixed forest with large oaks and hickories
nuthatch.role: The nuthatch reads the bark upside down, taking beetles, insect eggs and spiders from angles other birds never see. In autumn it wedges acorns and seeds into bark cracks to hammer open later, shifting seed around the woods. It cannot cut a hole of its own, so it moves into last year's downy woodpecker hole — no woodpecker, no nuthatch.
nuthatch.shelter: Natural cavities and old woodpecker holes in mature hardwoods; cannot excavate its own

octopus.diet: shore crabs, clams, mussels, snails and shrimp, cracked open or drilled through
octopus.fact: An octopus has three hearts, blue blood, and tastes everything it touches with its arms — and because the only hard part of it is its beak, one the size of a dinner plate can squeeze through a hole the size of a grape.
octopus.hint: Broken rock with gaps to hide in, and plenty of crabs. Leave the shell pile outside the den alone — that is how you know somebody is home.
octopus.name: Octopus
octopus.preferredHabitat: Rocky subtidal seafloor and deep tidepools with plenty of crevices and cold, clean water
octopus.role: The octopus is the top invertebrate hunter of the rocky shore, and the pile of emptied crab and clam shells outside its den is the easiest way to find one. It can change colour and skin texture in under a second to vanish against rock or kelp, despite being colourblind, and it will drill a neat hole through a stubborn clam and inject it to make the shell relax. Each octopus works through a huge number of crabs, which keeps the grazers and scavengers of the tidepools in check.
octopus.shelter: A crevice or empty shell it pulls a rock across behind itself, with a heap of emptied shells outside the door

opossum.diet: almost anything — insects, fruit, eggs, carrion, and an enormous number of ticks
opossum.fact: When an opossum plays dead it is not acting — it faints. The body goes stiff, the tongue lolls out and it gives off a smell like something long dead, and it cannot snap out of it for several minutes even if you walk away.
opossum.hint: Hollow wood to sleep the day away in and berries within a night's walk. It moves house constantly, so give it more than one option.
opossum.name: Opossum
opossum.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges with hollow wood, water nearby and plenty to scavenge
opossum.role: The meadow's clean-up crew. It eats what everything else has left, including carrion and vast quantities of ticks, and it is the only animal here that carries its young around on its back.
opossum.shelter: Sleeps the day out in a hollow log or a borrowed burrow, and rarely uses the same one twice

orca.diet: marine mammals — harbor seals above all, plus dolphins, sea lions and gray whale calves
orca.fact: Orcas live in families that never split up, and different families eat completely different food. The ones that hunt this coast are mammal specialists, and they go silent to do it — no clicks, no calls — because a seal can hear a talking orca coming from a long way off.
orca.hint: Deep water pressed right up against the shore and something big to hunt — so bring the seals back first, because the seals are what it comes for.
orca.name: Orca
orca.preferredHabitat: Cold deep water close inshore, along the drop-off and the kelp edge within reach of seal haul-outs
orca.role: The top of this coast, with nothing above it. A pod of mammal-hunting orcas patrols the drop-off where the seafloor falls away, listening at seal haul-outs and shadowing gray whales that pass through with calves in spring. When they come into a bay, every seal on the rocks goes still and silent.
orca.shelter: None ashore; rests at the surface in deep water with its family pod

painted-turtle.diet: mostly aquatic plants and algae as an adult; hatchlings and young turtles eat far more insects and carrion
painted-turtle.fact: A painted turtle spends the entire winter under the ice without taking a breath. It absorbs what oxygen it can through its back end, and when that runs short it dissolves minerals out of its own shell to stay alive until spring.
painted-turtle.hint: Still water, a soft mud bottom, and a log tilted up out of the water. No sunny log, no digestion.
painted-turtle.name: Painted Turtle
painted-turtle.role: The marsh's sunbather. A cold turtle cannot digest a thing, so a log in the sun is a feeding requirement rather than a luxury — and as painted turtles grow they flip from hunting insects to grazing plants.
painted-turtle.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; hauls out onto logs to bask

peregrine-falcon.diet: other birds taken in mid-air — white-tailed ptarmigan, rosy-finches, swifts, pipits and small ducks
peregrine-falcon.fact: A stooping peregrine hits about 380 km/h, which makes it the fastest animal alive — and it has bony cones in its nostrils that slow the air down so the dive does not burst its lungs.
peregrine-falcon.hint: A high ledge with loose gravel on it and open sky underneath. Do not build a nest — this one just kicks a dip in the grit.
peregrine-falcon.name: Peregrine Falcon
peregrine-falcon.preferredHabitat: Sheer cliffs and rock faces overlooking open ground with plenty of birds flying below
peregrine-falcon.role: The peregrine is the mountain's aerial hunter, and it takes almost all of its food in the air, striking from above with a closed fist rather than grabbing. Because it hunts birds and nothing else, it is a direct check on the flocks of finches, pipits and white-tailed ptarmigan feeding across the slopes. It needs an undisturbed cliff ledge and clear air below it, and nothing at all to build with — just loose gravel to scrape a hollow in.
peregrine-falcon.shelter: A bare scrape kicked into gravel on a high cliff ledge; it builds no nest at all

phainopepla.diet: mistletoe berries in winter, flying insects the rest of the year
phainopepla.fact: A phainopepla can put away more than a thousand mistletoe berries in a single day, and the seeds come out the other end still sticky — so the bird glues the next generation of mistletoe onto branches as it flies.
phainopepla.hint: Mistletoe in a mesquite is the whole story — the berries are dinner and the clump is the nest. It still comes down to drink.
phainopepla.name: Phainopepla
phainopepla.preferredHabitat: Mesquite stands carrying mistletoe, with water nearby
phainopepla.role: Mistletoe's one dependable gardener; almost nothing else will touch the berries. The plant only grows on mesquite, ironwood and acacia, so this glossy black bird with red eyes needs those trees as much as the mistletoe does. Out of berry season it snaps insects out of the air instead.
phainopepla.shelter: A small cup nest in a mesquite or ironwood, usually hidden in a clump of mistletoe

pika.diet: grasses, forbs, wildflowers and lichen, cut green and dried into winter haypiles
pika.fact: A pika spends its whole summer cutting flowers and grass and stacking them into little haystacks under the rocks, then eats its way through the pile in the dark under the snow.
pika.hint: Deep talus to vanish into with flowers a short dash away, then a haypile. Without cured hay it cannot last the winter.
pika.name: Pika
pika.preferredHabitat: Deep, stable talus with alpine flower turf right at its edge
pika.role: A hamster-shaped cousin of rabbits that lives in the gaps inside talus and squeaks at anything that comes near. It overheats after an hour of warm sun, so it works at dawn and dusk, and it has already vanished from the lower, hotter rockslides, which makes it the mountain's early warning system. Weasels, martens, foxes, wolverines and eagles all hunt it.
pika.shelter: Cool gaps deep within talus and broken rock

pileated-woodpecker.diet: carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae above all; also berries and nuts
pileated-woodpecker.fact: A pileated woodpecker chisels rectangular holes so deep into rotten trunks that a small tree can snap in half where it has been working.
pileated-woodpecker.hint: Big snags — plural, and thick — plus logs on the ground rotted hollow enough to tear straight into.
pileated-woodpecker.name: Pileated Woodpecker
pileated-woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Mature forest with large-diameter standing snags and plenty of big fallen logs on the ground
pileated-woodpecker.role: This is the forest's landlord. It carves a fresh nest hole every spring and never reuses the old one, and the leftovers become homes for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats and owls — none of which can make a hole themselves. It needs two things a tidied forest lacks: standing snags fat enough to hold a cavity, and fallen logs rotted soft enough to fill with carpenter ants. Bring those back and a dozen other species follow it in.
pileated-woodpecker.shelter: Excavates a new rectangular nest cavity each year in a large dead snag, and leaves last year's behind

pillbug.diet: dead leaves, rotting wood, grass thatch and fungal threads; also droppings and old bones for minerals
pillbug.fact: A pillbug is not an insect at all — it's a crustacean, closer kin to a crab than to a beetle, and it still breathes through gill-like flaps that have to stay wet.
pillbug.hint: Damp, dark and rotting is the whole recipe — a crumbling log, deep thatch, and ground that never dries right out. Roll one over and it curls into a ball.
pillbug.name: Pillbug
pillbug.preferredHabitat: Shaded, damp corners of meadow with rotting wood and a thick layer of dead plant litter
pillbug.role: Pillbugs work the night shift under logs and thatch, shredding dead leaves and soft rotten wood into crumbs small enough for fungi and bacteria to finish off. That shredding is the first step in turning last year's meadow into next year's soil. Garter snakes and killdeer hunt them, so the recycling crew feeds upward as well as downward.
pillbug.shelter: Hides by day under crumbling logs, flat stones and deep litter, where the air stays damp

pine-marten.diet: voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, insects and berries
pine-marten.fact: In winter a marten hunts inside the snowpack, in the hollow spaces between the drifts and the ground, where nothing else its size can follow it.
pine-marten.hint: You cannot build this one's habitat out of rocks and flowers. It needs a stand of real trees, dead wood on the ground, and hares already living there.
pine-marten.name: Pine Marten
pine-marten.preferredHabitat: Structurally complex treeline forest with big trees, dead wood and rock
pine-marten.role: A cat-sized weasel equally at home in the treetops and the snow tunnels, hunting voles, pikas, young hares and birds, with berries in late summer. Structure is what it needs above everything else, so a cleared slope empties of martens even while the prey is still there. Eagles catch it.
pine-marten.shelter: Dens in hollow logs, tree cavities and rock crevices, usually under deep snow

pipit.diet: mostly insects, springtails, spiders and their larvae, plus some seeds
pipit.fact: Wind sweeps insects up off the lowlands and dumps them on the snowfields, chilled and helpless. The pipit walks the edge of the melting snow eating a meal the weather delivered uphill.
pipit.hint: Open turf to walk and nest in, and a lingering snowbank with a dark line of debris along its edge. That stripe is the dinner table.
pipit.name: Pipit
pipit.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf and fellfield, especially along the edges of melting snow
pipit.role: A slim brown ground-walker that bobs its tail non-stop as it hunts across open turf. It nests in a scrape tucked beside a rock and feeds heavily on that stranded insect fallout, one of the strangest free lunches in the mountains. Foxes and ermines take it and its ground nests.
pipit.shelter: Ground nest of grass tucked into the turf beside a rock or a tussock

polyphemus-moth.diet: as a caterpillar, tree leaves — oak, birch, hickory, maple, willow. The adult moth has no working mouth and never eats anything at all.
polyphemus-moth.fact: The adult moth has no mouth. It cannot eat a single thing — everything it will ever spend finding a mate and laying eggs was eaten months earlier, by the caterpillar.
polyphemus-moth.hint: Broadleaf trees for the caterpillars to eat, and leaves left lying all winter for the cocoons hidden among them.
polyphemus-moth.name: Polyphemus Moth
polyphemus-moth.preferredHabitat: Broadleaf woodland and woodland edge with oak, birch and hickory, and an undisturbed litter layer beneath them.
polyphemus-moth.role: This moth stands for the caterpillar layer, the step nearly every forest bird depends on. Caterpillars turn tough, chewy tree leaves into soft protein, and it is caterpillars, not seeds, that woodland songbirds cram into their chicks. The adults that make it through feed bats at dusk. The cocoons spend all winter down in the fallen leaves, so a woodland raked bare in autumn throws next summer's moths out with the leaf bags.
polyphemus-moth.shelter: Spins a tough silk cocoon wrapped in a leaf; the cocoon falls with the leaves in autumn and overwinters on the forest floor.

porcupine.diet: almost entirely herbivorous — inner bark in winter, buds, twigs and leaves in summer — but gnaws shed antlers and bones for minerals
porcupine.fact: A porcupine cannot throw its quills — they simply stick to whatever bumps them. The barbed tips are coated in a natural antibiotic, so a porcupine that falls out of a tree and lands on itself usually heals up fine.
porcupine.hint: Hemlock and pine bark to live on through winter, and a hollow log or rock den to sleep the day away in.
porcupine.name: Porcupine
porcupine.preferredHabitat: Mixed and coniferous forest with thick-barked trees, especially hemlock, and rock or log dens below
porcupine.role: Porcupines improve the forest by damaging it. Stripping bark kills limbs and whole trees, and those dying trees become the snags, loose bark slabs and cavities that woodpeckers, bats and denning mammals move into — one animal's dinner is another animal's house. They eat the same nuts as squirrels and elk, and they are the entire reason a fisher would bother living here.
porcupine.shelter: Rock dens and hollow logs, reused season after season; also rests high in tree canopies

prairie-vole.diet: grasses, sedges, seeds and roots, plus bark in winter
prairie-vole.fact: Prairie voles pair up and stay together, and both parents raise the pups — which is why scientists who study bonding and loyalty end up studying this small brown rodent.
prairie-vole.hint: Thick unmown grass with clipped runways beneath it. This one arrives early, and almost everything with teeth or talons is waiting on it.
prairie-vole.name: Prairie Vole
prairie-vole.preferredHabitat: Dense grassy prairie and meadow with thick ground cover left standing
prairie-vole.role: The vole is the meadow's engine of small furry food. It mows narrow highways through the grass, breeds fast, and feeds hawks, owls, foxes, coyotes, snakes and badgers. The burrows it abandons get taken over by bumble bee queens and garter snakes, so it builds homes as well as filling stomachs.
prairie-vole.shelter: Shallow burrows and woven grass nests linked by clipped surface runways

praying-mantis.diet: live insects seized by ambush — grasshoppers, bees, butterflies and anything else that walks past
praying-mantis.fact: A mantis has one ear, in the middle of its chest, and it is tuned to bat calls. When it hears a bat hunting it folds its wings and power-dives out of the sky.
praying-mantis.hint: Leave stiff dead stems standing through the winter. That's where the foam egg case is glued, and cutting them back in autumn cuts next summer's brood.
praying-mantis.name: Praying Mantis
praying-mantis.preferredHabitat: Meadows and flowery edges with standing vegetation to ambush from
praying-mantis.role: A sit-still ambush hunter that snaps out its spined forelegs faster than you can blink and swivels its head almost right around to watch you. It is not a pest-control specialist — it takes whatever comes past, which means grasshoppers, but also bumble bees, leafcutter bees and monarch caterpillars. Bluebirds, meadowlarks, garter snakes and bats take it in turn.
praying-mantis.shelter: Perches motionless on plants; glues a foam egg case to a stiff standing stem for the winter

puffin.diet: small fish carried crosswise in its beak, plus shrimp and other small swimmers
puffin.fact: A puffin can hold a dozen fish crosswise in its beak at once without dropping any — backward-pointing spines on its tongue and the roof of its mouth pin each one while it catches the next.
puffin.hint: Soft turf on top of a cliff to dig a burrow into, and deep water below it full of small fish.
puffin.name: Puffin
puffin.preferredHabitat: Grassy clifftops above deep water, with soil soft enough to dig
puffin.role: A small seabird that lives almost its whole life out on the water and only comes ashore to nest, digging a burrow into the clifftop turf. Its beak only turns bright orange for the breeding season, then dulls again for winter.
puffin.shelter: A burrow dug a metre back into the turf on top of a sea cliff

purple-sea-urchin.diet: living kelp and surfgrass, drift kelp, and encrusting coralline algae
purple-sea-urchin.fact: A purple urchin chews a pit into solid rock with five teeth and then sits in it for years. On some reefs the urchins wear away more stone than the waves do.
purple-sea-urchin.hint: Kelp first — it has to have something to eat. Then think hard about what is going to eat it.
purple-sea-urchin.name: Purple Sea Urchin
purple-sea-urchin.preferredHabitat: Wave-exposed low intertidal and shallow subtidal rock near kelp
purple-sea-urchin.role: The grazer at the middle of this coast's most famous story. Fed on scraps of drift kelp and kept in check by otters, urchins are just one more part of a healthy forest. Take the predators away and they march up the rock, mow the kelp to bare stone, and leave an urchin barren behind them.
purple-sea-urchin.shelter: Pits it grinds into the rock itself with its teeth and spines

quail.diet: seeds, green leaves and cactus fruit — and, for the first weeks of life only, insects
quail.fact: One male stands sentry on a high branch with that comma of feathers bobbing on his forehead while the rest of the covey feeds below, and when he calls the alarm the whole group runs — quail would nearly always rather sprint than fly.
quail.hint: Thorny thickets to roost in and seeds to eat — and unlike most of this desert, water it can actually drink.
quail.name: Quail
quail.preferredHabitat: Thorny thickets along washes, within walking distance of water
quail.role: A sociable ground bird living on seeds and greens, with the chicks fattened on insects for their first few weeks. Unlike almost everything else here it genuinely has to drink, so coveys walk the same path to the same water every summer day. Coyotes and hawks take adults; ravens and roadrunners take eggs and chicks.
quail.shelter: A ground nest tucked under a shrub; the covey roosts up inside thorny cover at night

raccoon.diet: opportunistic: crayfish, insects, earthworms, frogs, eggs and fruit, with vertebrate prey a smaller share than most people assume
raccoon.fact: A raccoon sees with its hands. Its front paws carry four to five times more touch nerves than most mammals', and it will stare off in the opposite direction while its fingers read a stream bed.
raccoon.hint: A hollow den log and a stony shallow edge to feel around in. It hunts with its hands, not its eyes.
raccoon.name: Raccoon
raccoon.preferredHabitat: Moist forest beside water shallow enough to wade and feel around in
raccoon.role: The raccoon carries the stream into the woods: it feels out crayfish and insects in the shallows and unloads that energy up the bank, dropping fruit seeds as it goes. It is also this forest's great nest robber — the same crowd of cavities that lets wood ducks and flying squirrels move in hands a raccoon a list of doors to try.
raccoon.shelter: Hollow tree dens preferred; also rock crevices, burrows and buildings

ratsnake.diet: mice, voles, chipmunks and young squirrels, plus birds and eggs lifted straight out of nests
ratsnake.fact: A ratsnake can climb straight up a bare tree trunk with nothing to hold onto. It wedges the edges of its belly scales into the ridges in the bark and walks up the side of the tree, then robs the nest at the top.
ratsnake.hint: Big rough-barked trees are the whole trick — this snake hunts up them as much as under them. Leave a heap of rotting wood chips at the foot of a stump for her eggs, and skip the pond; she does not need one.
ratsnake.name: Ratsnake
ratsnake.preferredHabitat: Old woods and woodland edges with big rough-barked trees to climb and rodents underneath them
ratsnake.role: The forest's rodent brake, and the only hunter here that works in three dimensions. On the ground it takes mice, voles and chipmunks by the dozen; up in the canopy it raids old woodpecker holes and songbird nests, which is why every bird in earshot mobs it. It kills by wrapping and squeezing, not venom, and when it is startled it freezes into a stiff kinked shape that looks exactly like a fallen branch. She never sits on her eggs — she buries them in rotting wood and lets the heat of the rot do the incubating. Foxes, fishers and great horned owls eat it.
ratsnake.shelter: Hollow trunks, rot pockets and stump cavities; the eggs go into a warm heap of rotting wood chips

rattlesnake.diet: rodents and small mammals, with birds and lizards taken now and then
rattlesnake.fact: A rattlesnake adds a new rattle segment every time it sheds, but the old ones keep snapping off — so counting the rattles tells you nothing whatsoever about its age.
rattlesnake.hint: A deep winter den it can come back to every single year, warm rock to wait on, and rodents on the move nearby.
rattlesnake.name: Rattlesnake
rattlesnake.preferredHabitat: Rocky shelter within striking distance of busy rodent trails
rattlesnake.role: An ambush hunter that lies beside a rodent trail for days, strikes, lets go, then follows the scent trail to the body. It may eat only once a month, which makes it a slow but relentless brake on the rodent population. Every winter it goes back to the same rock den it used last year, and the year before that.
rattlesnake.shelter: Rock crevices and burrows; a deep frost-free fissure all winter

raven.diet: carrion above all, plus eggs, nestlings, young reptiles, insects and cactus fruit
raven.fact: Ravens remember individual human faces and hold the grudge for years, and a pair will run a con together — one bird makes a nuisance of itself while the other robs the food.
raven.hint: They follow whatever gets left lying around: a carcass, a tall perch, something to drink. That is all they ask for — which is exactly the trouble.
raven.name: Raven
raven.preferredHabitat: Open desert with tall nest structures and a reliable food supply
raven.role: The cleanup crew, and the biggest human story in the biome. Roads, rubbish tips, farms and power poles hand ravens free food, water and nest platforms, so there are now far more of them than this desert could ever feed by itself — and all those extra ravens eat baby tortoises, whose shells stay soft for years. Cutting off the free lunch is now a real part of saving the tortoise.
raven.shelter: Bulky stick nests on cliffs and in tall cactus and ironwoods — and, more and more, on power poles

red-fox.diet: voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds and insects, rounded out with berries and carrion
red-fox.fact: A fox listening for a vole under deep grass or snow lines itself up facing magnetic north before it leaps — and the trick only seems to help when it cannot see the prey at all.
red-fox.hint: This one comes back once the small animals do — and she needs an old burrow she can widen into a nursery.
red-fox.name: Red Fox
red-fox.preferredHabitat: Meadows, field edges and hedgerows across open country
red-fox.role: A stalk-and-pounce generalist that keeps rodent and rabbit numbers down and fills the gaps with insects, berries and whatever it finds already dead. It rarely digs a den from scratch — it widens an old ground squirrel or badger burrow instead. Great horned owls take its kits, and now that coyotes are back, foxes have to give ground.
red-fox.shelter: Enlarges a burrow another animal dug into a natal den; also uses brush and hollows

red-tailed-hawk.diet: mostly small mammals — voles, ground squirrels, rabbits — plus birds and snakes
red-tailed-hawk.fact: That screaming eagle cry in every film is a red-tailed hawk. Actual bald eagles sound like squeaky gulls, so the movies quietly swapped them.
red-tailed-hawk.hint: A tall tree crown for the stick nest, open grass to hunt over, and a meadow already full of small mammals. It takes its water from its prey.
red-tailed-hawk.name: Red-tailed Hawk
red-tailed-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open country seen from above: grassland, fields and meadows
red-tailed-hawk.role: The daylight hunter over this meadow, either circling on broad flat wings or sitting on a pole staring at the grass. It is heavy and powerful and built for taking prey off the ground — voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, snakes — not for chasing birds through the air. The huge stick nest it builds gets inherited by a great horned owl the very next winter.
red-tailed-hawk.shelter: A bulky stick nest in the crown of a tall tree or on a cliff ledge

red-winged-blackbird.diet: insects in summer, seeds and grain the rest of the year
red-winged-blackbird.fact: A male red-wing can switch his scarlet shoulder patches on and off. Flared wide they start fights; tucked away under the black feathers they let him slip through a rival's territory completely unnoticed.
red-winged-blackbird.hint: Standing stems with water beneath them. The nest is stitched around the reeds and the water underneath is the burglar alarm.
red-winged-blackbird.name: Red-winged Blackbird
red-winged-blackbird.preferredHabitat: Dense cattail and reed stands with water underneath
red-winged-blackbird.role: The loudest bird in the marsh and the first one back in spring. It hunts insects all summer and switches to seeds for the rest of the year, and it winds its nest around standing stems with water underneath — a moat the mink will not cross.
red-winged-blackbird.shelter: Cup nests wound around several upright stems standing in water

river-cooter.diet: pondweed, algae, water lily leaves and fallen fruit; hatchlings take insects before switching to plants
river-cooter.fact: Whether a cooter's eggs hatch into males or females depends on how warm the nest is, not on the eggs themselves — a cool nest makes brothers, a warm one makes sisters.
river-cooter.hint: Logs in the sun to bask on and a bare warm bank to bury eggs in. One that cannot get warm cannot digest its dinner.
river-cooter.name: River Cooter
river-cooter.preferredHabitat: Slow, plant-filled water with logs to bask on and an open sunlit bank to lay eggs in
river-cooter.role: The cooter is the wetland's big plant-eating turtle, cropping the underwater meadows and keeping them from choking the shallows, and passing seeds out intact somewhere else. It has to bask for hours to get warm enough to digest all that plant food, which is why a good log stacked with turtles is a sign of a working marsh. Its eggs and hatchlings feed almost everything else, so it lays a lot of them.
river-cooter.shelter: Sleeps wedged under submerged logs and root tangles; spends the winter buried in the mud of the pond bottom

river-otter.diet: fish, crayfish, mussels, frogs and other aquatic animals
river-otter.fact: An otter has around 350,000 hairs packed into every square centimetre of its fur — more than most animals have on their entire body. It is the air trapped in all that fur, not fat, that keeps an otter warm in freezing water.
river-otter.hint: Lots of connected clean water, plenty of fish and crayfish, and an old beaver-made bank den with an underwater door.
river-otter.name: River Otter
river-otter.preferredHabitat: Clean, connected water rich in fish and slow prey
river-otter.role: The best swimmer in the marsh and the top hunter under the surface. Otters need a lot of clean connected water and a den they did not dig themselves, so an otter here means the beaver came back first — and it means the eagles finally have someone worth robbing.
river-otter.shelter: Bank dens with underwater entrances — usually a beaver's old lodge or burrow

roadrunner.diet: lizards, big insects, millipedes, scorpions, tarantulas, small birds, rodents and snakes
roadrunner.fact: A roadrunner can outrun you — over 30 km an hour on two legs — and it kills a rattlesnake by grabbing it behind the head and beating it against a rock until it stops moving.
roadrunner.hint: Open ground to run flat out on and a thorn thicket to nest in, with lizards and big crawlers to chase between the two.
roadrunner.name: Roadrunner
roadrunner.preferredHabitat: Open running ground broken up by thorny thickets
roadrunner.role: The daytime terror of anything small and quick: lizards, tarantulas, scorpions, millipedes, other birds, and one of the very few birds anywhere that will pick a fight with a rattlesnake. It needs both halves of its home — open ground to sprint across and a thorn thicket high enough to keep its chicks out of a mountain lion's reach.
roadrunner.shelter: A bulky stick nest a metre or two up inside a thorny shrub or cholla

rock-squirrel.diet: seeds, berries and green shoots, plus underground fungi, insects and the occasional egg
rock-squirrel.fact: Everyone calls it a giant chipmunk, but look at its face — no stripes on the cheeks. And it does not just nap through winter: it cools until its body is barely above freezing and its heart slows to a few beats a minute.
rock-squirrel.hint: It is only above ground for half the year, so look for it in the warm months. Seed-heavy flowers to fatten on, rock to duck into, and diggable ground under a boulder for the long sleep.
rock-squirrel.name: Rock Squirrel
rock-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Sunny rocky slopes, talus edges and open dwarf-pine ground at and above the tree line
rock-squirrel.role: A stripe-backed seed machine that spends the short summer eating itself round, then vanishes underground for half the year. It buries seeds all over the slope and forgets enough of them to replant it, and it digs up and eats underground fungi, so the spores ride through its gut and get planted somewhere new. Ermines, martens, lynx and eagles all hunt it, and the tunnels it abandons become shelter for toads and beetles.
rock-squirrel.shelter: A burrow driven in under a boulder or a fallen log, with a grass-lined sleeping chamber at the far end

sand-dollar.diet: algae, plankton and scraps of food picked out of the sand grain by grain
sand-dollar.fact: A living sand dollar is not white and smooth — it is purple and covered in tiny moving spines it uses to walk and to pass food along to its mouth. The white disc with the flower pattern is its skeleton, after everything else has washed away.
sand-dollar.hint: Clean rippled sand just below the tide line, somewhere sheltered enough that the current is gentle.
sand-dollar.name: Sand Dollar
sand-dollar.preferredHabitat: Sheltered sandy bottoms just below the low tide line, where the current is gentle
sand-dollar.role: A whole bed of them stands half-buried on edge like coins in a slot, all leaning into the current to catch what drifts past. Where the water is rougher they lie flat instead so they do not get rolled away.
sand-dollar.shelter: Half buried on edge in rippled sand, in beds of hundreds at a time

sanderling.diet: beach hoppers, mole crabs, amphipods, worms and small molluscs
sanderling.fact: Sanderlings spend the whole day sprinting at the sea and running away from it, chasing each wave out to grab whatever it uncovered and fleeing the next one before it buries them.
sanderling.hint: The wet strip where the waves run out, with open sand behind it. Do not plant anything here — this bird feeds where the water slides.
sanderling.name: Sanderling
sanderling.preferredHabitat: The wet swash zone of an open sandy beach
sanderling.role: A specialist of the sliding strip of water at the sea's edge, feeding on the small crustaceans the surf keeps turning over. Its flocks live or die on how much life the wrack line produces, so a beach that is groomed clean is a beach without sanderlings.
sanderling.shelter: Open beach above the surf line

sandhill-crane.diet: grains, tubers, insects, crayfish and small animals
sandhill-crane.fact: Cranes dance to choose a partner — leaping, bowing and flinging sticks in the air — and once they pair up they usually stay together for life. Their bugling carries more than two kilometres because the windpipe is coiled up inside the breastbone like a trumpet.
sandhill-crane.hint: This one wants space and quiet. Build a wide, well-balanced marsh and heap a nest mound up above the waterline.
sandhill-crane.name: Sandhill Crane
sandhill-crane.role: The tallest bird on the marsh and the last one to arrive. Cranes probe the mud for tubers and snap up frogs, crayfish and insects, and they will only settle where the water is wide, quiet and genuinely healthy.
sandhill-crane.shelter: Large ground mounds of piled marsh plants standing in shallow water

scorpion.diet: millipedes, termites, crickets, spiders, tarantulas and other scorpions
scorpion.fact: Scorpions glow an eerie blue-green under ultraviolet light, and after decades of looking at it nobody can say for certain why.
scorpion.hint: Rocks are only the doormat. What it really needs is soil deep and loose enough to dig metres straight down into.
scorpion.name: Scorpion
scorpion.preferredHabitat: Loose diggable soil with litter and stone cover to hunt across at night
scorpion.role: The heavyweight of the night shift. Big, hairy and unhurried, it takes millipedes, termites, spiders and even tarantulas, which are its own size. The rocks are only its day cover — what actually keeps it alive is a spiral burrow driven metres straight down, where it sits out most of the year. Owls and roadrunners are the ones that get it.
scorpion.shelter: A spiral burrow it digs itself, as much as two and a half metres deep

sea-otter.diet: sea urchins above all, plus mussels, crabs and sea stars
sea-otter.fact: A sea otter has no blubber at all — just the thickest fur on Earth, about a million hairs in a patch the size of a postage stamp — so it spends hours a day combing air into its coat, and wraps itself in kelp so it does not drift away while it sleeps.
sea-otter.hint: Living kelp forest to wrap up in, calm water to groom in, and urchins and shellfish to eat. Dead kelp on the sand is no use to it.
sea-otter.name: Sea Otter
sea-otter.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with abundant shellfish and calm rafting water
sea-otter.role: The animal this whole coast hangs on. By eating urchins it stops them mowing the kelp down to bare rock, so the forest and everything sheltering in it survives. Remove the otter and the urchins multiply, the kelp goes, and what is left is a barren. Note what it rafts in: living canopy, not dead wrack on the beach.
sea-otter.shelter: Rafts wrapped in living surface kelp canopy, in coves calm enough to groom in

sea-star.diet: mussels above all, plus barnacles, limpets, chitons, snails and small urchins
sea-star.fact: This is the animal the word 'keystone' was invented for. Take the sea stars off a shore and within a couple of years the mussels spread down over everything else — which is precisely what happened when a wasting disease melted these stars by the million along thousands of miles of coast.
sea-star.hint: Build the mussel bed first, and build it big. It lives down in among the shells, along the bottom edge where the bed gives way to open rock.
sea-star.name: Sea Star
sea-star.preferredHabitat: Wave-washed rocky intertidal with mussel beds above and surge below
sea-star.role: The rocky shore's most famous predator. Working upward from the low zone and eating mussels as it goes, it decides where the mussel bed stops, and that leaves bare space on the rock for barnacles, algae, anemones and dozens of other species. Remove it and the mussels simply take everything.
sea-star.shelter: Damp surge channels and rock crevices at the lower edge of the mussel bed

sea-turtle.diet: seagrass above all — eelgrass and surfgrass — plus sea lettuce and other soft algae
sea-turtle.fact: Adult green sea turtles are the only sea turtles that eat plants, and their jaws are serrated like bread knives for sawing through seagrass. They crop the same patch again and again, which keeps it short and tender — a turtle basically mows a lawn on the seafloor.
sea-turtle.hint: This one comes for the grazing, not the sand, so do not build it a nest beach. Warm summer water, a cropped grazing lawn out in the eelgrass, and quiet bottom to sleep on between meals.
sea-turtle.name: Sea Turtle
sea-turtle.preferredHabitat: Warm summer water in a sheltered bay with seagrass meadows to graze
sea-turtle.role: A summer visitor that swims in from warmer water to eat, not to nest — no turtle lays eggs on a cool coast like this one. Grazing adults keep the seagrass cropped and growing fresh instead of going long and shaggy, and they are the only animal here besides the brant that eats a seagrass meadow for a living.
sea-turtle.shelter: Sleeps wedged under ledges or resting on quiet sand and gravel bottom between grazing trips

shore-crab.diet: mostly algae and drift kelp, plus detritus, worms, snails and carrion
shore-crab.fact: The shore crab spends more than half its life out of the sea, breathing air on dry rock, and only nips back to a pool now and then to wet its gills.
shore-crab.hint: Barely any water. High rock, deep cracks to wedge into, and one pool nearby to duck into when it needs a drink.
shore-crab.name: Shore Crab
shore-crab.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal and splash zone, often out of the water altogether
shore-crab.role: The busiest scavenger on the highest rocks, scraping surfaces clean of algae and hauling away anything that dies. It is also breakfast for gulls, oystercatchers and turnstones, and one of the very first animals to reappear on a shore that is coming back to life.

skunk.diet: beetle grubs and insects dug out of the soil, plus eggs, berries and mice
skunk.fact: A skunk would much rather not spray you. First it stamps its front feet, then it hisses, then it does a handstand — and only if you ignore all three does it turn around and fire, accurately, from about three metres.
skunk.hint: Soft, diggable earth full of grubs, and a hollow log to sleep the day away in. It wants somewhere to dig more than somewhere to hide.
skunk.name: Skunk
skunk.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and clearings with soft diggable ground and plenty of cover
skunk.role: The forest's night gardener. It spends the dark hours digging little cone-shaped holes across the floor hunting beetle grubs, turning over the soil as it goes, and almost nothing dares hunt it — except the great horned owl, which has no sense of smell worth mentioning.
skunk.shelter: A borrowed burrow or a hollow under a log, plugged with leaves in the coldest weeks

snail.diet: dead leaves, soft rotting stems, and the algae film on damp stones
snail.fact: A snail carries its own house and can shut the door behind it — when things get dry it glues itself to a stone and sleeps until it rains, sometimes for months.
snail.hint: A shady damp corner where leaves are allowed to pile up and rot. It wants the mess, not the tidy bit.
snail.name: Snail
snail.preferredHabitat: Shady, damp corners with leaf litter and something chalky to rasp at
snail.role: Snails are the meadow's slow recyclers. They shred fallen leaves into crumbs that fungi and soil life can finish off, and their shells give calcium back to the ground when they die.
snail.shelter: Seals itself to the underside of a damp log or stone and waits out dry weather

snapping-turtle.diet: carrion, fish, crayfish, aquatic plants and almost anything else it can catch
snapping-turtle.fact: A snapping turtle is too big to pull into its own shell, so it does not bother trying. Underwater it is calm and shy and will swim away from you — the famous snap only comes out when it is stranded on dry land with nowhere left to hide.
snapping-turtle.hint: Deep still water with a soft bottom, plus a warm sandy rise above the waterline for the females to dig their nests in.
snapping-turtle.name: Snapping Turtle
snapping-turtle.preferredHabitat: Deep still water with a soft mud bottom and a sandy rise to nest on
snapping-turtle.role: The marsh's bulldozer and its clean-up crew, walking the bottom eating carrion, plants, fish and the occasional duckling. Grown adults are almost untouchable; it is the eggs everything digs up, which is why one good nest bank matters more than any single old turtle.
snapping-turtle.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; females travel overland to sandy banks to nest

snow-bunting.diet: seeds blown onto the snow, plus insects in the short summer
snow-bunting.fact: Snow buntings nest further north than any other songbird on Earth, tucked so deep in rock cracks that the male has to feed the female in the dark while she sits.
snow-bunting.hint: A deep, dry crack in the rock out of the wind, and open stony ground nearby where the snow blows clear.
snow-bunting.name: Snow Bunting
snow-bunting.preferredHabitat: Windswept ridges and fellfield where the snow blows clear
snow-bunting.role: A small bird that treats a blizzard as ordinary weather. Flocks drift across bare ridges picking up seed the wind has stranded on the snow, and they turn from white to warm brown as the season turns.
snow-bunting.shelter: Deep in a rock crevice, lined with feathers and fur against the cold

snow-flea.diet: dead leaves and stems, fungal threads, pollen, and the pink algae that grow on old snow
snow-flea.fact: On a mild winter day snow fleas pour out onto the snow in their thousands, like somebody spilled pepper across the drift. Their blood is full of natural antifreeze, so they keep moving when everything else is frozen stiff.
snow-flea.hint: A mat of litter under melting snow is enough to start.
snow-flea.name: Snow Flea
snow-flea.preferredHabitat: Damp alpine turf, moss cushions and snowmelt litter, plus the surface of late-lying snow on warm days
snow-flea.role: The clean-up crew, and the reason last year's leaves do not simply pile up forever. Snow fleas shred dead stems and graze fungal threads into soil, and they keep at it all winter in the dark gap between the snowpack and the ground. Pipits, finches, chickadees, bluebirds, nutcrackers and toads all snap them up.
snow-flea.shelter: Wet leaf litter, moss cushions, and the hollow gap between the snowpack and the ground in winter

snowshoe-hare.diet: green plants in summer; willow and juniper twigs, buds, bark and conifer needles in winter
snowshoe-hare.fact: The hare changes colour by the calendar, not the weather. Shortening days flip its coat white whether the snow has turned up or not, so a warm autumn can leave a white hare sitting on brown ground.
snowshoe-hare.hint: Low tangled cover it can freeze motionless inside, a scraped hollow under the krummholz to sit out the day, and willow to browse in winter. Open ground with a rock pile on it is the opposite of what it wants. It eats snow instead of drinking.
snowshoe-hare.name: Snowshoe Hare
snowshoe-hare.preferredHabitat: Dense krummholz, juniper and willow thickets at and just below treeline
snowshoe-hare.role: A browsing hare of thick treeline cover with back feet like snowshoes that hold it up on top of drifts. It freezes rather than runs, so tangled low cover is everything to it, and willow twigs get it through the winter. Martens, foxes, eagles, wolverines and lions all hunt it.
snowshoe-hare.shelter: Shallow 'forms' scraped under dense shrubs and low conifer branches

snowy-plover.diet: beach invertebrates: beach hoppers, kelp flies and their larvae, small crustaceans and molluscs
snowy-plover.fact: A snowy plover's entire nest is a dent in bare sand lined with a few shell chips. The chicks run within hours of hatching, and freeze flat as pebbles the moment a shadow crosses them.
snowy-plover.hint: No water, no planting. Bare open sand, a roped-off patch where nobody treads, and driftwood for the chicks to hide beside.
snowy-plover.name: Snowy Plover
snowy-plover.preferredHabitat: Wide, flat, sparsely vegetated open sand above the tide line
snowy-plover.role: A threatened beach nester that feeds on tiny invertebrates along the sand and the wrack. It will not nest where it cannot see a predator coming, which makes it one of the very few animals here that thick planting drives away rather than attracts — the kindest thing you can build it is emptiness nobody walks through.
snowy-plover.shelter: A shallow scrape on open sand, sometimes lined with shell fragments; chicks shelter beside driftwood and wrack

song-sparrow.diet: insects and spiders in summer; seeds, berries and grass heads the rest of the year
song-sparrow.fact: Every song sparrow makes up its own tunes. A young male listens to the neighbours, then invents his own set of eight or ten and sings them for life, so you can learn to tell individual birds apart by ear.
song-sparrow.hint: A damp, messy corner with a thick tussock to hide a nest in and berries close by. It likes the untidy bits best.
song-sparrow.name: Song Sparrow
song-sparrow.preferredHabitat: Brushy, slightly damp edges — the messy strip between open grass and thicker cover
song-sparrow.role: One of the first birds to find a mending meadow and one of the last to leave it. It works the scruffy middle ground, eating insects all summer and switching to seeds in winter.
song-sparrow.shelter: A cup of grass tucked low in a shrub or a thick tussock, close to damp ground

tiger-salamander.diet: worms, insects, freshwater shrimp and other small invertebrates; larvae take tadpoles
tiger-salamander.fact: Tiger salamanders spend most of their lives alone underground, then walk back on the first warm rainy night of spring to the exact pool they hatched in — and if that pool starts drying too fast, some larvae grow oversized heads and start eating their own brothers and sisters.
tiger-salamander.hint: Dig the vernal pools well away from the fish pools and let them dry right out in summer. Fish and it larvae cannot share water.
tiger-salamander.name: Tiger Salamander
tiger-salamander.preferredHabitat: Fishless seasonal pools with soft banks
tiger-salamander.role: A fat, blotched, black-and-gold hunter that only breeds where fish cannot live. Its larvae race to grow legs before the pool dries, which is a bet they can only win in water no minnow could survive.
tiger-salamander.shelter: Damp burrows in soft ground near fishless breeding pools

towhee.diet: insects, spiders and millipedes kicked out of the leaf litter, plus seeds, berries and bits of acorn
towhee.fact: That loud rustling in the dead leaves usually isn't a deer — it's a bird the size of your hand, kicking backwards with both feet at once to flip the leaves over and see what's underneath.
towhee.hint: Thick young brush standing over a deep, unraked leaf layer. The nest goes on the ground, so the tangle above it has to be dense enough to hide it.
towhee.name: Towhee
towhee.preferredHabitat: Brushy tangles, forest edges and sunlit gaps where young growth is thick and the ground is deep in fallen leaves
towhee.role: The towhee works a layer nothing else in this forest bothers with: the top couple of inches of dead leaves. Its two-footed backwards kick turns litter over and over while it hunts the insects, spiders and millipedes hiding there, and the seeds and berries it swallows come back out along the brushy edges. Because the nest sits flat on the ground, the towhee feeds foxes and snakes — and it can only nest where the brush overhead is thick enough to hide a cup of grass.
towhee.shelter: Nests on the ground in dead leaves beneath a bramble or dense shrub, the cup sunk level with the surface

tree-squirrel.diet: acorns, hickory nuts, tree buds, samaras and fungi; occasional insects and bird eggs
tree-squirrel.fact: A squirrel buries thousands of nuts a year and forgets a good share of them. The forgotten ones grow into trees, so most squirrels accidentally plant a forest in a lifetime.
tree-squirrel.hint: Oaks to feed and bury from, a high fork for a summer drey, and a big tree to den in over winter.
tree-squirrel.name: Tree Squirrel
tree-squirrel.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous or mixed forest rich in oaks and hickories
tree-squirrel.role: The gray squirrel is a seed eater who keeps failing at his own plan, and the woods are better for it: acorns buried and never dug up again are how oaks climb hills and fill gaps. Its droppings scatter fungal spores, its leafy summer dreys get taken over by great horned owls, and being the commonest mid-sized animal in the forest it is on the menu of nearly every predator here.
tree-squirrel.shelter: Tree cavity dens in winter and leaf-and-twig dreys built high in the canopy in summer

water-strider.diet: insects and spiders trapped in the surface film, plus mosquito larvae hanging just underneath it.
water-strider.fact: Water striders do not swim — they stand on the water. Thousands of tiny hairs on each foot trap air and refuse to get wet, and the strider reads ripples the way a spider reads its web to find insects thrashing on the surface.
water-strider.hint: This one needs calm. Find a pocket of water the wind cannot ruffle, with floating stems on it to rest and lay eggs on.
water-strider.name: Water Strider
water-strider.preferredHabitat: Smooth, calm pockets of open water out of the wind, with floating stems to rest and lay eggs on.
water-strider.role: The marsh's surface patrol, and one of the first animals back once the water is clean and still. Striders skate over the film eating whatever falls in and cannot climb out, and they are themselves easy pickings for minnows, frogs, dragonflies and blackbirds.
water-strider.shelter: Sheltered, wind-free water; overwinters tucked under bank litter and floating debris.

western-meadowlark.diet: mostly insects in summer — beetles, grasshoppers, crickets — and seeds in winter
western-meadowlark.fact: A meadowlark weaves a roof over its nest and a covered tunnel leading in, so from above there is nothing to see at all — just grass.
western-meadowlark.hint: Wide unbroken native grass and a perch to sing from. Skip the shrubs here — woody cover is exactly what pushes this one out.
western-meadowlark.name: Western Meadowlark
western-meadowlark.preferredHabitat: Wide native grassland with song perches and no shrubs moving in
western-meadowlark.role: A grassland bird through and through. It eats grasshoppers, crickets and beetles by the hundred all summer and switches to seed in winter, and it needs real open space — as shrubs and trees creep in, meadowlarks quietly vanish. A plump bird that nests on the ground is a favourite of hawks, foxes, badgers and coyotes.
western-meadowlark.shelter: A domed grass nest woven on the ground, usually with a covered runway leading in

white-tailed-ptarmigan.diet: buds, twigs, leaves, seeds and flowers; in winter almost entirely willow buds and twigs
white-tailed-ptarmigan.fact: It grows feathers on its feet for winter, built-in snowshoes, and then dives into a snowdrift to sleep, because inside the drift it is far warmer than out in the wind.
white-tailed-ptarmigan.hint: Willow is the whole winter for this one, and a soft deep drift is its bedroom. It eats snow instead of drinking, and it has no use at all for a flower planter.
white-tailed-ptarmigan.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
white-tailed-ptarmigan.preferredHabitat: Alpine tundra above treeline year-round, dropping into sheltered willow basins in winter
white-tailed-ptarmigan.role: A grouse that spends its entire life above the trees, mottled brown in summer and pure white in winter and so well hidden that people walk within a metre without seeing one. Willow buds are almost its whole winter diet. Eagles, foxes, weasels, martens and wolverines hunt it and its chicks.
white-tailed-ptarmigan.shelter: Camouflaged ground scrapes among lichen-covered rock, and burrows dug into soft snow to roost

white-throated-swift.diet: flying insects only — moths, beetles, flies and drifting swarms of ants, all taken in mid-air
white-throated-swift.fact: It does everything in the air. It eats in the air, drinks in the air, and pairs mate in mid-air — locking together and tumbling hundreds of feet down the cliff face before they let go.
white-throated-swift.hint: A narrow crack in a cliff to sleep in and a lot of open air in front of it. It never lands to feed and it drinks on the wing, so any pool it can skim will do.
white-throated-swift.name: White-throated Swift
white-throated-swift.preferredHabitat: Sheer cliffs and broken crags with a lot of open air in front of them to hunt in
white-throated-swift.role: A blade-shaped bird that lives in the sky above the mountain, hoovering up moths, beetles and whatever else the wind lifts, at speeds that make it one of the fastest birds alive in level flight. Its feet only cling, never perch, so it has to fold itself into a crack in a cliff at night, and it sticks the nest in place with its own saliva. Because it eats only what is flying, a swift working the ridge is proof the insect life below has come back. Almost nothing is quick enough to catch one.
white-throated-swift.shelter: A cup of feathers glued with its own spit into a narrow crack in a cliff face

wolverine.diet: marmots, hares and white-tailed ptarmigan when it can catch them, frozen carcasses when it cannot, and berries in late summer
wolverine.fact: A wolverine can smell a dead animal buried under three metres of snow, dig it out, and then drive a bear off it, all in a body about the size of a small dog.
wolverine.hint: It needs space and snow, not scenery. Give it drifts deep enough to last into late spring for the den and the larder, broken rock to travel through, and marmots and hares already on the mountain.
wolverine.name: Wolverine
wolverine.preferredHabitat: Big, empty, high country with talus and broken rock, and snow that lasts into late spring
wolverine.role: The largest weasel in the world and the mountain's great scavenger, now the top hunter on these peaks. It roams enormous distances, kills marmots, hares and white-tailed ptarmigan when it gets the chance and lives off frozen carcasses when it does not, cracking frozen bone with jaws built for exactly that. Snow is its refrigerator: it stores food in drifts and dens deep inside them, so a female can only raise kits where the snowpack holds into late spring. That makes it the first animal to go when winters get short — and nothing up here is willing to argue with it over a carcass.
wolverine.shelter: Tunnels dug metres down into deep spring drifts, usually around a fallen boulder or log, with food stored in side chambers

wood-duck.diet: acorns, seeds and aquatic plants; ducklings eat insects and snails for their first weeks
