wood-duck.fact: A wood duckling leaves home the day after it hatches by jumping out of a hole up to fifty feet up, bouncing off the ground or water, and walking away unhurt.
wood-duck.hint: An old woodpecker hole in a snag standing over quiet water, with oaks nearby for acorns.
wood-duck.name: Wood Duck
wood-duck.preferredHabitat: Wooded ponds, sloughs and slow backwaters with big cavity trees standing in or near the water
wood-duck.role: The wood duck is the clearest borrower in the forest: it cannot make a hole and cannot nest without one, so it turns up only after the woodpeckers do. It ferries acorns and pond-plant seeds between the woods and the water, and it feeds owls, raccoons and foxes. Wood ducks nearly vanished a century ago, and what still limits them is holes.
wood-duck.shelter: Obligate cavity nester — old woodpecker holes and natural hollows in trees over or beside water

wood-frog.diet: beetles, spiders, slugs, flies and other small forest-floor invertebrates
wood-frog.fact: A wood frog freezes solid every winter. Its heart stops, two thirds of the water in its body turns to ice, and in spring it thaws out and hops away.
wood-frog.hint: A pool that dries up in summer is the good kind — no fish means the tadpoles live. Keep deep leaves nearby for them to freeze in.
wood-frog.name: Wood Frog
wood-frog.preferredHabitat: Damp deciduous forest with fishless woodland pools that fill in spring and dry out by late summer
wood-frog.role: Wood frogs are the first amphibian to call in spring, breeding in temporary pools that dry up before fish can ever live in them — which is exactly why the tadpoles survive. Sugar flooding the blood keeps their cells from bursting while they are frozen, so they can hibernate under a few centimetres of leaves. As adults they eat their way through the invertebrates of the leaf litter and are eaten in turn by snakes and raccoons, moving forest-floor energy up the food chain.
wood-frog.shelter: Shallow leaf litter and loose duff on the forest floor — it does not burrow below the frost line

woodpecker.diet: mostly insects — beetle larvae, ants, caterpillars — with some berries and sap
woodpecker.fact: A downy woodpecker weighs about as much as four sheets of paper — light enough to hang off a dead weed stem and drill into it, which no bigger woodpecker can manage.
woodpecker.hint: Small dead stubs with the wood already gone soft. It cannot chisel healthy timber, so leave the rotting stuff standing.
woodpecker.name: Woodpecker
woodpecker.preferredHabitat: Open deciduous and mixed woodland with small dead stubs and dead limbs on living trees
woodpecker.role: The downy cuts the small holes. It can only chisel wood that fungi have already softened, so it waits on the decomposers — and the nuthatches and chickadees, which cannot cut a hole at all, wait on it. It works bark crevices and dead twigs for beetle grubs and ants that heavier woodpeckers can't reach, and its eggs feed climbing snakes.
woodpecker.shelter: Excavates its own cavity in a small dead stub, usually in wood already softened by fungus; roosts in cavities year-round

yellow-bellied-marmot.diet: grasses, flowering plants and seeds, eaten hard through a short summer
yellow-bellied-marmot.fact: A yellow-bellied marmot sleeps for about eight months of the year and wakes up weighing half what it did when it went to bed.
yellow-bellied-marmot.hint: Soil deep enough to dig, a boulder to dig under, and a lot of green within waddling distance. Do not go looking after early autumn, because it is underground until spring.
yellow-bellied-marmot.name: Yellow-bellied Marmot
yellow-bellied-marmot.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf broken by boulders, with diggable soil underneath
yellow-bellied-marmot.role: A fat, sun-basking rodent that eats meadow plants flat out through a short summer and whistles from a boulder the moment a shadow crosses. Its old burrows become fox dens, bumble bee nests and toad hideouts, so a surprising amount of the mountain depends on its digging. Eagles, foxes, martens, wolverines and lions hunt it.
yellow-bellied-marmot.shelter: Deep, many-chambered burrows dug beneath boulders, below the frost line

alpine.description: A trampled alpine slope. The wildflower turf is worn through and the talus is silent.
alpine.name: Graywind Heights
alpine.restorationGoal: Restore alpine turf, snowmelt pools, and rocky shelter for high-country animals.

coastal.description: A scoured stretch of coast where the open ocean breaks along the western edge. The dunes have washed out and the tidepools are empty, but sea glass, kelp, driftwood, and the odd pearl still wash up on the tide.
coastal.name: Pelican Shore
coastal.restorationGoal: Anchor the dunes, restore tidepools and kelp wrack, and reopen the shore to coastal life.

desert.description: An overgrazed desert flat. Without brush or burrows, the heat keeps everything away.
desert.name: Redstone Scrubland
desert.restorationGoal: Replant cactus and brush, build shade and burrows, and bring the desert back to life.

forest.description: A logged-over woodland. The big trees are gone, the understory is bare, and the birds have moved on.
forest.name: Old Hollow Forest
forest.restorationGoal: Rebuild the understory, raise nesting trees and deadwood, and welcome the forest animals back.

meadow.description: A once-flowering meadow beside your home, now dusty and quiet. Native grasses were stripped away and the pollinators left with them.
meadow.name: Willow Meadow
meadow.restorationGoal: Replant grasses and wildflowers, add water and shelter, and help 10 meadow animals return.

wetland.description: A drained marsh. Old channels are dry, the reeds are gone, and the water that remains is murky.
wetland.name: Rushwater Wetland
wetland.restorationGoal: Restore shallow water, reed beds, and mud banks so wetland life can return.
